## 1. Āhuneyyavagga
## 1. Paṭhama Āhuneyyasutta
1. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus, "Bhikkhus." "Venerable Sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the six?
Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is neither elated nor depressed, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
Having smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having felt a tactile object with the body...
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither elated nor depressed, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of these six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."
The Blessed One said this. Those bhikkhus were delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.
The First.
248:
First Sutta.
## 2. Dutiya Āhuneyyasutta
2. "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the six?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu exercises the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though through water; he walks on water without breaking through as though on earth; he travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma world. (1)
With the divine ear element (dibbasota), which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near. (2)
He knows the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with his own mind. He knows a mind with lust (rāga) as a mind with lust; he knows a mind without lust as a mind without lust; he knows a mind with hatred (dosa) as a mind with hatred; he knows a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; he knows a mind with delusion (moha) as a mind with delusion; he knows a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; he knows a constricted mind as a constricted mind; he knows a scattered mind as a scattered mind; he knows an exalted mind (mahaggata) as an exalted mind; he knows an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; he knows a surpassable mind (sa-uttara) as a surpassable mind; he knows an unsurpassable mind (anuttara/lokuttara) as an unsurpassable mind; he knows a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; he knows an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; he knows a liberated mind as a liberated mind; he knows an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind. (3)
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. (4)
With the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:
'These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of noble ones, wrong in their views, giving effect to wrong views in their actions, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of misery...'
249:
With the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell. 

'But these beings, sirs, who are possessed of good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who are not revilers of noble ones, who hold right view and undertake actions based on right view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. (5)

'With the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein.' (6)

Monks, a monk possessed of these six qualities is worthy of gifts... p ... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

The Second Sutta.

## 3-Indriya Sutta

3. Monks, a monk possessed of six qualities is worthy of gifts... p ... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

What are the six?

He is possessed of the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

With the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein.

Monks, a monk possessed of these six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

The Third Sutta.

## 5-Pathama Ājānīya Sutta

5. Monks, a king's auspicious thoroughbred steed possessed of six factors is worthy of a king, a royal possession, and is reckoned as a factor of the king.

What are the six?

Here, monks, a king's auspicious thoroughbred steed:

Is patient with forms.
Is patient with sounds.
Is patient with smells.
Is patient with tastes.
Is patient with tactile objects.
And is possessed of beauty.

Monks, a king's auspicious thoroughbred steed possessed of these six factors is worthy of a king, a royal possession, and is reckoned as a factor of the king.

In the same way, monks, a monk possessed of six qualities is worthy of gifts... p ... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

What are the six?

Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a monk:

Is patient with forms.
Is patient with sounds.
Is patient with smells.
Is patient with tastes.
Is patient with tactile objects.
Is patient with mental phenomena.

Monks, a monk possessed of these six qualities is worthy of gifts... p ... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

## 7. Third Ājānīya Sutta
7. "Monks, possessed of six factors, a king's noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a factor of a king. What are the six?

Monks, herein, a king's noble thoroughbred horse is patient of forms, patient of sounds, patient of smells, patient of tastes, patient of tactile objects, and is endowed with speed. Monks, possessed of these six factors, a king's noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a factor of a king.

In the same way, monks, possessed of six qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the six?

Herein, monks, a bhikkhu is patient of forms, patient of sounds, patient of smells, patient of tastes, patient of tactile objects, and patient of mental phenomena (dhammas). Monks, possessed of these six qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Anuttariya Sutta
8. "Monks, there are these six unsurpassable things. What are the six?

The unsurpassable seeing, the unsurpassable hearing, the unsurpassable gain, the unsurpassable training, the unsurpassable service, and the unsurpassable recollection. Monks, these are the six unsurpassable things."

Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta
9. "Monks, there are these six bases of recollection (which are the causes of welfare and happiness). What are the six?

Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue (sīla), recollection of generosity (cāga), and recollection of the devas (recalling one's own qualities of faith, etc., which are similar to those of the devas). Monks, these are the six bases of recollection."

Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Mahānāma Sutta
10. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park. Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, when a noble disciple has attained the fruit and has understood the teaching (the three trainings), in what way does he frequently dwell?"

"Mahānāma, when a noble disciple has attained the fruit and has understood the teaching, he frequently dwells in this way (to be described):"
252:
"Mahānāma, herein, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly self-awakened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.'

Mahānāma, when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred, not obsessed by delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, with the Tathāgata as the object.

Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straight mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is glad, rapture arises; for one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil; one with a tranquil body experiences happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.

Mahānāma, this noble disciple is said to be one who dwells evenly among a generation that has reached unevenness, who dwells unafflicted among a generation that is afflicted, and who, having entered the stream of Dhamma (insight wisdom), develops the recollection of the Buddha.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, worthy of application, to be personally realized by the wise.'

Mahānāma, when a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred, not obsessed by delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, with the Dhamma as the object.

Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straight mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is glad, rapture arises; for one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil; one with a tranquil body experiences happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.

Mahānāma, this noble disciple is said to be one who dwells evenly among a generation that has reached unevenness,"

He is said to be one who dwells at ease among a distressed generation, who has entered the stream of the Dhamma (known as insight knowledge) and develops the recollection of the Dhamma (Dhammānussati). (2)

Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha:

This Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples—the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—is worthy of gifts brought from afar, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings intended for the next world, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha, his mind is not obsessed by greed, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is upright, fixed on the qualities of the Saṅgha.

Mahānāma, a noble disciple with an upright mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is glad, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.

Mahānāma, this noble disciple is said to be one who dwells at ease among a troubled generation, who dwells without distress among a distressed generation, who has entered the stream of the Dhamma (known as insight knowledge) and develops the recollection of the Saṅgha (Saṅghānussati). (3)

Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects his own virtues: which are unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unblemished, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and leading to concentration.

Mahānāma, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the qualities of his virtue, his mind is not obsessed by greed, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is upright, fixed on the qualities of virtue.

Mahānāma, a noble disciple with an upright mind gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is glad, rapture arises. Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple develops the recollection of deities (taking them as witnesses to his own qualities of faith, etc.): "There are the deities of the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa deities, the Yāma deities, the Tusita deities, the Nimmānarati deities, the Paranimmitavasavatti deities, the Brahma-kāyika deities, and deities beyond these. Such virtue... such learning... such generosity... such wisdom as those deities possessed, because of which they passed away from this human world and were reborn in that world of deities, such wisdom is also found in me."

## 3. Nissāraṇīya Sutta

13. Bhikkhus, there are these six elements of deliverance. What are the six?

Bhikkhus, here in this Teaching, a bhikkhu might say:

"I have developed the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti), cultivated it, made it a vehicle, made it a basis, established it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it; yet ill-will (byāpāda) still obsesses my mind and remains."

That bhikkhu should be told: "Do not say so! Venerable sir, do not say so. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that when the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, ill-will should still obsess the mind and remain. This is not possible. For this, friend—the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness—is the escape from ill-will."

Bhikkhus, here in this Teaching, a bhikkhu might say:

"I have developed the deliverance of mind through compassion (karuṇā cetovimutti), cultivated it, made it a vehicle, made it a basis, established it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it; yet cruelty (vihiṃsā) still obsesses my mind and remains."

That bhikkhu should be told: "Do not say so! Venerable sir, do not say so. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that when the deliverance of mind through compassion has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, cruelty should still obsess the mind and remain. This is not possible. For this, friend—the deliverance of mind through compassion—is the escape from cruelty."

Bhikkhus, here in this Teaching, a bhikkhu might say:
258:
"I have developed the deliverance of mind through appreciative joy (muditā cetovimutti), cultivated it, made it a vehicle, made it a basis, established it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it; yet discontent (arati) still obsesses my mind and remains."

That bhikkhu should be told: "Do not say so! Venerable sir, do not say so. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that when the deliverance of mind through appreciative joy has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, discontent should still obsess the mind and remain. This is not possible. For this, friend—the deliverance of mind through appreciative joy—is the escape from discontent."

Bhikkhus, here in this Teaching, a bhikkhu might say:

"I have developed the deliverance of mind through equanimity (upekkhā cetovimutti), cultivated it, made it a vehicle, made it a basis, established it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it; yet lust (rāga) still obsesses my mind and remains."

That bhikkhu should be told: "Do not say so! Venerable sir, do not say so. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that when the deliverance of mind through equanimity has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, lust should still obsess the mind and remain. This is not possible. For this, friend—the deliverance of mind through equanimity—is the escape from lust."

Bhikkhus, here in this Teaching, a bhikkhu might say:

"I have developed the signless deliverance of mind (animitta cetovimutti), cultivated it, made it a vehicle, made it a basis, established it, consolidated it, and properly undertaken it; yet my consciousness still follows after signs (nimitta)."

That bhikkhu should be told: "Do not say so! Venerable sir, do not say so. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that when the signless deliverance of mind has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, consciousness should still follow after signs. This is not possible. For this, friend—the signless deliverance of mind—is the escape from all signs."
259:
“Monks, in this Teaching, a monk might say: ‘Though the conceit “I am” has gone from me, and I do not regard “This I am,” yet the thorn of doubt and uncertainty remains, obsessing my mind.’

He should be told: ‘Do not say so, friend. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for misrepresentation of the Blessed One is not good. The Blessed One would not speak thus. Friend, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that when the conceit “I am” has gone and one does not regard “This I am,” the thorn of doubt and uncertainty should still obsess the mind; such a thing is impossible. For, friend, the uprooting of the conceit “I am” is the escape from the thorn of doubt and uncertainty.’

Monks, these are the six elements of deliverance.”

The third sutta.

## 4. Bhaddaka Sutta

14. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: “Friends, monks.” “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

“Friends, in whatever way a monk lives such that his death is not auspicious and his passing away is not auspicious, in that way the monk lives.

And how, friends, does a monk live in such a way that his death is not auspicious and his passing away is not auspicious?

Friends, in this Teaching, a monk delights in work, takes pleasure in work, and is devoted to delighting in work. He delights in talk, takes pleasure in talk, and is devoted to delighting in talk. He delights in sleep, takes pleasure in sleep, and is devoted to delighting in sleep. He delights in company, takes pleasure in company, and is devoted to delighting in company. He delights in social contact (of five kinds), takes pleasure in social contact, and is devoted to delighting in social contact. He delights in proliferation (papañca), takes pleasure in proliferation, and is devoted to delighting in proliferation.

In this way, friends, a monk lives such that his death is not auspicious and his passing away is not auspicious.

Friends, this monk is called one who delights in identity (sakkāya), who does not abandon identity for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.”
260:
“Friends, in whatever way a monk lives such that his death is auspicious and his passing away is auspicious, in that way the monk lives.

And how, friends, does a monk live in such a way that his death is auspicious and his passing away is auspicious?

Friends, in this Teaching, a monk does not delight in work, does not take pleasure in work, and is not devoted to delighting in work. He does not delight in talk, does not take pleasure in talk, and is not devoted to delighting in talk. He does not delight in sleep, does not take pleasure in sleep, and is not devoted to delighting in sleep. He does not delight in company, does not take pleasure in company, and is not devoted to delighting in company. He does not delight in social contact (of five kinds), does not take pleasure in social contact, and is not devoted to delighting in social contact. He does not delight in proliferation (papañca), does not take pleasure in proliferation, and is not devoted to delighting in proliferation.

In this way, friends, a monk lives such that his death is auspicious and his passing away is auspicious.

Friends, this monk is called one who delights in Nibbāna, who abandons identity for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.

“The person who is devoted to proliferation,
A beast who delights in proliferation,
He misses Nibbāna,
The unsurpassed security from bondage.

“But he who, having given up proliferation,
Delights in the state of non-proliferation,
He attains Nibbāna,
The unsurpassed security from bondage.”

The fourth sutta.

## 5. Anutappiya Sutta

15. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks:

“Friends, in whatever way a monk lives such that he must feel remorse when he dies, in that way the monk lives.

And how, friends, does a monk live in such a way that he must feel remorse when he dies?

Friends, in this Teaching, a monk delights in work, takes pleasure in work, and is devoted to delighting in work. He delights in talk. He delights in sleep. He delights in company. He delights in social contact (of five kinds). He delights in proliferation (papañca), takes pleasure in proliferation, and is devoted to delighting in proliferation.

In this way, friends, a monk lives such that he must feel remorse when he dies.”
261:
Friends, this monk is called one who delights in identity (sakkāya), who does not abandon identity for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.

Friends, in whatever way a monk lives so that his death is without remorse, in that way he lives. And how, friends, does a monk live so that his death is without remorse?

Here, friends, a monk does not delight in work, does not find pleasure in work, does not engage in delighting in work. He does not delight in talk... sleep... company... social contact... proliferation (papañca), does not find pleasure in proliferation, does not engage in delighting in proliferation.

In this way, friends, a monk lives so that his death is without remorse. This monk is called one who delights in Nibbāna, who abandons identity for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.

One who is engaged in proliferation, a beast delighting in proliferation, misses Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage. But one who, having given up proliferation, delights in the state of non-proliferation, attains Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.

Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Nakulapitu Sutta

16. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. At that time, the householder Nakulapita was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the housewife Nakulamata said to the householder Nakulapita:

"Householder, do not die with concern. To die with concern is painful, householder, and death with concern is censured by the Blessed One.

Householder, it may be that you think: 'After my passing, the housewife Nakulamata will not be able to support the young children or maintain the household.'

Householder, it should not be seen in this way. Householder, I am skilled in spinning and carding wool.

Householder, after your passing, I will be able to support the young children and maintain the household."
262: 'Householder, therefore do not die with longing. Death for one with longing is painful, and death with longing is criticized by the Blessed One. (1) Householder, it might occur to you: "The housemother Nakulamātā will take another husband after I pass away." But, householder, you should not see it like that. Householder, you know as well as I do that for sixteen years we have lived the holy life of a householder (gahaṭṭhaka brahmacariya). Therefore, householder, do not die with longing. Death for one with longing is painful, and death with longing is criticized by the Blessed One. (2) Householder, it might occur to you: "The housemother Nakulamātā will not desire to see the Blessed One or the Saṅgha of monks after I pass away." But, householder, you should not see it like that. Householder, after you pass away, I will desire to see the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks even more. Therefore, householder, do not die with longing. Death for one with longing is painful, and death with longing is criticized by the Blessed One. ## 7. Soppa Sutta

17. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his solitary seclusion and went to the assembly hall, where he sat down on the prepared seat.

The Venerable Sāriputta also rose from his solitary seclusion in the evening, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down at one side.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna... the Venerable Mahākassapa... the Venerable Mahākaccāna... the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika... the Venerable Mahācunda... the Venerable Mahākappina... the Venerable Anuruddha... the Venerable Revata... and the Venerable Ānanda also rose from their solitary seclusion in the evening, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down at one side.

Then the Blessed One, having spent much of the night sitting there, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Those venerable ones also, not long after the Blessed One had departed, rose from their seats and went to their respective dwellings.

However, those newly ordained monks in this Dhamma-Vinaya, who had not been ordained for long, slept snoring loudly until sunrise.
265:
The Blessed One, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, saw those monks sleeping and snoring until sunrise. Having seen them, he went to the assembly hall and sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

“Monks, where is Sāriputta? Where is Mahāmoggallāna? Where is Mahākassapa? Where is Mahākaccāna? Where is Mahākoṭṭhika? Where is Mahācunda? Where is Mahākappina? Where is Anuruddha? Where is Revata? Where is Ānanda? Monks, where have those elder disciples gone?”

“Venerable Sir, those venerable ones, not long after the Blessed One had departed, rose from their seats and went to their respective dwellings,” they replied.

“Monks, why do you sleep and snore until sunrise, [thinking] ‘The elder monks have not returned’? 

Monks, what do you think? Have you ever seen or heard of an anointed kshatriya king who, being addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of sloth as much as he likes, and while ruling for his whole life, is dear and pleasing to the people?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Good, monks! I too, monks, have never seen or heard of an anointed kshatriya king who, being addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of sloth as much as he likes, and while ruling for his whole life, is dear and pleasing to the people.”

“Monks, what do you think? Have you ever seen or heard of a district ruler... [and so on]... an inherited town ruler, a general, a village headman, or a guild leader who, being addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of sloth as much as he likes, and while acting as guild leader for his whole life, is dear and pleasing to the guild?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Good, monks! I too, monks, have never seen or heard of a guild leader who, being addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of sloth as much as he likes, and while acting as guild leader for his whole life, is dear and pleasing to the guild.”

“Monks, what do you think?”
266:
“Have you ever seen or heard of an ascetic or a brahmin who, being addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of sloth as much as he likes, with unguarded doors in the sense faculties, immoderate in eating, not devoted to wakefulness, not contemplating wholesome states, and not devoted to the practice of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammas) in the first and last watches of the night—yet, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, attains, and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind (arahattaphala-citta) and liberation by wisdom (arahattaphala-paññā) in this very life?”

“No, venerable sir.”

“Good, monks! I too, monks, have never seen or heard of an ascetic or a brahmin who, being addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of sloth as much as he likes, with unguarded doors in the sense faculties, immoderate in eating, not devoted to wakefulness, not contemplating wholesome states, and not devoted to the practice of the factors of enlightenment in the first and last watches of the night—yet, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, attains, and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life.”

“Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will be those with guarded doors in the sense faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, contemplating wholesome states, and we will dwell devoted to the practice of the factors of enlightenment in the first and last watches of the night.’

Monks, thus should you train yourselves.”

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Macchabandha Sutta

18. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large community of monks. While traveling along the highway, the Blessed One saw in a certain place a fisherman killing fish and selling them. Having seen this, he left the road, sat down on a prepared seat at the foot of a certain tree, and addressed the monks:

“Monks, do you see this fisherman killing fish and selling them?”

“Yes, venerable sir.”

“Monks, what do you think? Have you ever seen or heard of a fisherman who, by killing fish and selling them, through that work and that livelihood, becomes one who rides an elephant, or a horse, or a chariot, or a vehicle, or one who enjoys wealth, or one who lives presiding over a great mass of wealth?”

“No, venerable sir.”
267:
“Monks, it is well. I too have never seen nor heard of a fisherman who, by repeatedly killing and selling fish, through that work and that livelihood, becomes one who rides an elephant, a horse, a chariot, or a vehicle, or one who enjoys wealth, or one who dwells presiding over a great mass of wealth. Why is that? Because, monks, that fisherman looks upon those fish brought for slaughter with an evil mind; therefore, he does not ride an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a vehicle, nor does he enjoy wealth, nor does he dwell presiding over a great mass of wealth.”

“Monks, what do you think? Have you ever seen or heard of a cattle butcher who, by repeatedly killing and selling cattle, through that work and that livelihood, becomes one who rides an elephant, a horse, a chariot, or a vehicle, or one who enjoys wealth, or one who dwells presiding over a great mass of wealth?”

“No, Venerable Sir.”

“Monks, it is well. I too have never seen nor heard of a cattle butcher who, by repeatedly killing and selling cattle, through that work and that livelihood, becomes one who rides an elephant, a horse, a chariot, or a vehicle, or one who enjoys wealth, or one who dwells presiding over a great mass of wealth. Why is that? Because, monks, that cattle butcher looks upon those cattle brought for slaughter with an evil mind; therefore, he does not ride an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a vehicle, nor does he enjoy wealth, nor does he dwell presiding over a great mass of wealth.”

“Monks, what do you think? Have you ever seen or heard of a sheep butcher... [pe]... a pig butcher... [pe]... a fowler... [pe]... a hunter who, by repeatedly killing and selling wild animals, through that work and that livelihood, becomes one who rides an elephant, a horse, a chariot, or a vehicle, or one who enjoys wealth, or one who dwells presiding over a great mass of wealth?”

“No, Venerable Sir.”

“Monks, it is well. I too have never seen nor heard of a hunter who, by repeatedly killing and selling wild animals, through that work and that livelihood, becomes one who rides an elephant, a horse, a chariot, or a vehicle, or one who enjoys wealth, or one who dwells presiding over a great mass of wealth. Why is that? Because, monks, that hunter looks upon those wild animals brought for slaughter with an evil mind; therefore, he does not ride an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a vehicle, nor does he enjoy wealth, nor does he dwell presiding over a great mass of wealth.”
268:
“Monks, because that hunter looks upon even those animals brought for slaughter with an evil mind, he does not ride an elephant, nor a horse, nor a chariot, nor a vehicle, nor does he enjoy wealth, nor does he dwell presiding over a great mass of wealth.

What then can be said of one who looks upon a human being brought for slaughter with an evil mind? Monks, that is true; looking upon a human being with an evil mind for the purpose of killing leads to that person's harm and suffering for a long time. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell.”

The eighth discourse.

## 9. Paṭhama Maraṇassati Sutta

19. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Nātika in the Brick House (Giñjakāvasatha). There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!” “Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Monks, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it merges into the Deathless and has the Deathless as its consummation. Monks, do you develop mindfulness of death?”

When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death.”

“Monk, in what way do you develop mindfulness of death?”

“Venerable Sir, here I have this thought: ‘O, that I might live for a day and a night, that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would be done by me.’ Venerable Sir, it is in this way that I develop mindfulness of death.”

Then another monk said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death.”

“Monk, in what way do you develop mindfulness of death?”

“Venerable Sir, here I have this thought: ‘O, that I might live for just one day, that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would be done by me.’ Venerable Sir, it is in this way that I develop mindfulness of death.”
269:
Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death."
"And how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"
"Venerable Sir, here it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for the duration of eating one meal of almsfood, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death."

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death."
"And how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"
"Venerable Sir, here it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for the duration of chewing and swallowing four or five morsels of food, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death."

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death."
"And how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"
"Venerable Sir, here it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for the duration of chewing and swallowing just one morsel of food, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death."

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death."
"And how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"
"Venerable Sir, here it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for the duration of breathing in and out, or breathing out and in, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death."

When this had been said, the Blessed One said to those monks:
"Monks, the monk who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'Oh, that I might live for a day and a night, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me';
And the monk who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'Oh, that I might live for a day...'
271:
“A scorpion might bite me, or a centipede might bite me. Because of that, I might die; that would be an obstacle for me. Or I might stumble and fall, or the food I have eaten might disagree with me, or my bile might be disturbed, or my phlegm might be disturbed, or sharp winds might pierce me. Because of that, I might die; that would be an obstacle for me.”

Monks, that bhikkhu should reflect thus: “Are there any evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that would be an obstacle for me if I were to die during the night?”

Monks, if a bhikkhu, while reflecting, knows thus: “There are evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that would be an obstacle for me if I were to die during the night,” then, monks, that bhikkhu should put forth extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil, unwholesome states.

Monks, just as a person whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would put forth extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish the fire on his clothes or head; even so, monks, that bhikkhu should put forth extraordinary desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil, unwholesome states.

## 3. Anuttariyavagga

## 1. Sāmaka Sutta

21. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Sāmagāma near the Pokkharaṇiya lotus pond.
273:
Then, when the night was far spent, a certain deity of stunning beauty, illuminating the whole of Pokkharaṇiya with his radiance, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, these three things lead to the decline of a monk.
Which three?
Delight in work,
delight in talk,
delight in sleep.
Venerable sir, these three things lead to the decline of a monk."

That deity said this. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, knowing "The Teacher has approved of me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and vanished right there.

Then, when the night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, this night a certain deity, when the night was far spent, of stunning beauty, illuminating the whole of Pokkharaṇiya with his radiance, approached me. Having approached and paid homage to me, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, monks, that deity said this to me:

'Venerable sir, these three things lead to the decline of a monk.
Which three?
Delight in work,
delight in talk,
delight in sleep.
Venerable sir, these three things lead to the decline of a monk.'

Monks, that deity said this, and having said it, paid homage to me, circumambulated me, and vanished right there.

Monks, it is a loss for those monks, it is their misfortune, that even the deities know them to be declining in wholesome states.

Monks, I will also teach other things that lead to decline, the parihāniya-dhammas. Listen and pay close attention; I will speak."

"Yes, venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One taught this Dhamma:

"Monks, which are the three things that lead to decline?
Delight in company,
being difficult to admonish,
evil friendship.
Monks, these are the three things that lead to decline.

Monks, whoever in the past declined in wholesome states, all of them declined in wholesome states because of these six things.

Monks, whoever in the future will decline in wholesome states, all of them will decline in wholesome states because of these six things."
274:
"Monks, whoever at present is declining in wholesome states, all of them are declining in wholesome states because of these six things."

The First Sutta.

## 2. Aparihāniya Sutta

22. "Monks, I will teach these six things that lead to non-decline. Listen and pay close attention; I will speak."

"And which, monks, are the six things that lead to non-decline?
Not delighting in work,
not delighting in talk,
not delighting in sleep,
not delighting in company,
being easy to admonish,
good friendship.
Monks, these are the six things that lead to non-decline.

Monks, whoever in the past did not decline in wholesome states, all of them did not decline because of these six things.

Monks, whoever in the future will not decline in wholesome states, all of them will not decline because of these six things.

Monks, whoever at present is not declining in wholesome states, all of them do not decline because of these six things."

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Bhaya Sutta

23. "Monks, 'fear' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'suffering' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'disease' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'a boil' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'attachment' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'mire' is a designation for sensual pleasures.

And why, monks, is 'fear' a designation for sensual pleasures?

Monks, this being who is infatuated by sensual lust and bound by the lust of desire is not freed from fear in the present life, nor is he freed from fear in the life to come. Therefore, 'fear' is a designation for sensual pleasures.

And why, monks, is 'suffering' ... (as above) ... 'disease' ... 'a boil' ... 'attachment' ... 'mire' a designation for sensual pleasures?

Monks, this being who is infatuated by sensual lust and bound by the lust of desire is not freed from the mire in the present life, nor is he freed from the mire in the life to come. Therefore, 'mire' is a designation for sensual pleasures."

Fear, suffering, disease, a boil,
Both attachment and the mire;
These are called sensual pleasures,
Wherein the worldling is stuck.
275:
“Having seen danger in clinging, in the origin of birth and death, they are liberated without clinging, in the destruction of birth and death. They have reached safety, are happy, extinguished in this very life, transcended all enmity and fear, and have overcome all suffering.”

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Himavanta Sutta
24. “Monks, a monk endowed with six qualities could split even the Himalayas, the king of mountains, let alone wretched ignorance! What six?

Here, monks, a monk is skilled in entering concentration (samādhi), skilled in staying in concentration, skilled in emerging from concentration, skilled in the readiness for concentration, skilled in the object of concentration, and skilled in the directing of concentration.

Monks, a monk endowed with these six qualities could split even the Himalayas, the king of mountains, let alone wretched ignorance!”

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Anussatiṭṭhāna Sutta
25. “Monks, there are these six bases of recollection. What six?

Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata: ‘The Blessed One is an Arahant, perfectly self-enlightened... [as in the formula]... teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’

Monks, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Tathāgata, his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight; it has departed from, is released from, and has emerged from greed (gedha).

Monks, ‘greed’ is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Monks, by taking this recollection of the Buddha as an object, some beings in this world are purified.

Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One... [as in the formula]... to be personally experienced by the wise.’
276:
Monks, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Dhamma, his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight; it has departed from, is released from, and has emerged from greed.

Monks, ‘greed’ is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Monks, by taking this recollection of the Dhamma as an object, some beings in this world are purified.

Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well... [as in the formula]... the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’

Monks, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Saṅgha, his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight; it has departed from, is released from, and has emerged from greed.

Monks, ‘greed’ is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Monks, by taking this recollection of the Saṅgha as an object, some beings in this world are purified.

Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects his own virtues (sīla) which are unbroken, untattered... [as in the formula]... leading to concentration.

Monks, at the time when a noble disciple recollects his virtues, his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight; it has departed from, is released from, and has emerged from greed.

Monks, ‘greed’ is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Monks, by taking this recollection of virtue as an object, some beings in this world are purified.

Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects his own generosity (cāga): ‘It is a gain for me, it is a great gain for me... [as in the formula]... devoted to charity and sharing.’ ... [as before] ... some beings in this world are purified.

Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects the deities, taking them as witnesses for his own qualities such as faith: ‘There are the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tusita gods, the gods who delight in creation, the gods who wield power over others’ creations, the gods of the Brahma-group, and gods beyond these. Those deities, endowed with such faith, passed away from here and were reborn there. Such faith is also found in me. Those deities, endowed with such virtue... learning... generosity... wisdom, passed away from here and were reborn there. Such wisdom is also found in me.’
277:
"Such wisdom is also found in me." (Thus he recollects repeatedly.)

Monks, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom of both himself and those deities, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is simply straight; it has emerged from, is released from, and has risen above ‘greed’ (gedha). 

Monks, this name ‘greed’ is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure. 

Monks, it is by taking this recollection of deities (devatānussati) as an object that some beings in this world are purified (from defilements). 

Monks, these are the six bases of recollection. (Thus he said.)

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Mahākaccāna Sutta

26. On that occasion, the Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed the monks: "Friends, monks!" "Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāna. The Venerable Mahākaccāna said this:

Friends, it is wonderful! It is amazing! How the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, has discovered the attainment of an opening in the midst of confinement—for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the passing away of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna—that is, these six bases of recollection.

What are the six?

Friends, in this teaching, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Blessed One:

"The Blessed One is such because he is an Arahant... because he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā)." (Thus he recollects repeatedly.)

Friends, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Blessed One, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. At that time, his mind is simply straight; it has emerged from, is released from, and has risen above ‘greed’. Friends, this name ‘greed’ is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure. 

Friends, that noble disciple dwells with a mind like the sky—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without ill will. 

Friends, it is by taking this mind as an object that some beings in this world are of such a nature to be purified. 

Furthermore, friends, a noble disciple recollects the qualities of the Dhamma:

"The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One... to be personally experienced by the wise." (Thus he recollects repeatedly.)

Friends, at the time when a noble disciple recollects his own virtues, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, his mind is not obsessed by hatred, his mind is not obsessed by delusion. Friends, at the time when a noble disciple recollects his own quality of generosity, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust...
279:
The mind is not overwhelmed by ill-will, nor is the mind overwhelmed by delusion. At that time, his mind is straight; it has emerged from, is released from, and has risen above 'gedha'. Friends, 'gedha' is a term for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
