How the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has discovered the opening in the midst of confinement for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna—that is, these six recollections.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Paṭhamasamaya Sutta

27. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, he said to the Blessed One:
280:
"Venerable sir, how many are the occasions for approaching to see a monk who is worthy of esteem (manobhāvanīya)?"

"Monk, there are these six occasions for approaching to see a monk who is worthy of esteem.

What are the six?

Here, monk, when a monk dwells with a mind overwhelmed by sensual lust, obsessed by sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the sensual lust that has arisen, at that time he should approach a monk who is worthy of esteem and say:

'Friend, I dwell with a mind overwhelmed by sensual lust, obsessed by sensual lust, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the sensual lust that has arisen. It would be good if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual lust.'

The monk who is worthy of esteem then teaches him the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual lust.

Monk, this is the first occasion for approaching to see a monk who is worthy of esteem.

Furthermore, monk, when a monk dwells with a mind overwhelmed by ill-will, obsessed by ill-will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the ill-will that has arisen, at that time he should approach a monk who is worthy of esteem and say:

'Friend, I dwell with a mind overwhelmed by ill-will, obsessed by ill-will, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the ill-will that has arisen. It would be good if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of ill-will.'

The monk who is worthy of esteem then teaches him the Dhamma for the abandoning of ill-will.

Monk, this is the second occasion for approaching to see a monk who is worthy of esteem.

Furthermore, monk, when a monk dwells with a mind overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, obsessed by sloth and torpor, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the sloth and torpor that has arisen, at that time he should approach a monk who is worthy of esteem and say:

'Friend, I dwell with a mind overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, obsessed by sloth and torpor, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the sloth and torpor that has arisen. It would be good if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of sloth and torpor.'"
281:
To that bhikkhu, the monk who has developed his mind teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of sloth and torpor (thina-middha).
Bhikkhu, this is the third occasion for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.

Bhikkhu, another way: at a time when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse; at that time, he should approach a monk who has developed his mind and speak to him thus:
“Venerable sir, I dwell with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. I request you, venerable sir, please teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.”
To that bhikkhu, the monk who has developed his mind teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.
Bhikkhu, this is the fourth occasion for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.

Bhikkhu, another way: at a time when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt (vicikicchā), overwhelmed by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt; at that time, he should approach a monk who has developed his mind and speak to him thus:
“Venerable sir, I dwell with a mind obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. I request you, venerable sir, please teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of doubt.”
To that bhikkhu, the monk who has developed his mind teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of doubt.
Bhikkhu, this is the fifth occasion for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.

Bhikkhu, another way: at a time when a bhikkhu does not understand that sign (nimitta) by depending on which and by attending to which the destruction of the taints (āsavas) occurs without hindrance; at that time, he should approach a monk who has developed his mind and speak to him thus:
“Venerable sir, I do not understand that sign by depending on which and by attending to which the destruction of the taints occurs without hindrance. I request you, venerable sir, please teach me the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.”
To that bhikkhu, the monk who has developed his mind teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.
Bhikkhu, this is the sixth occasion for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.
Bhikkhu, these are the six occasions for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.

(The seventh sutta ends.)
282:
The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Dutiya Samaya Sutta

28. On one occasion, many elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. At that time, in the afternoon, after returning from their alms round, as the elder bhikkhus were sitting together and assembled in the circular hall, this intermediate conversation arose:
“Friends, what is the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind?”

When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, when a monk who has developed his mind has returned from his alms round after the meal, has washed his feet, and sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him (towards the meditation subject)—that is the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to that (first) bhikkhu:
“Friend, that is not the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.
Friends, when a monk who has developed his mind has returned from his alms round after the meal, has washed his feet, and sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him—at that time, his fatigue from walking for alms has not yet subsided, and his fatigue from eating has not yet subsided. Therefore, that is not the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.
Friend, when a monk who has developed his mind has risen from seclusion in the evening and sits in the shade of the monastery, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him—that is the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to that (second) bhikkhu:
“Friend, that is not the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.
Friend, when a monk who has developed his mind has risen from seclusion in the evening and sits in the shade of the monastery, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him—at that time, the very sign of concentration (samādhinimitta) that he attended to during the day still recurs to him frequently. Therefore, that is not the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.
“Friend, when a monk who has developed his mind has risen in the last watch of the night and sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him—that is the right time for approaching to see a monk who has developed his mind.”
283:
When this was said, another monk said to that (third) monk: "Friend, that is not the time to approach a monk worthy of esteem for a visit. Friend, when a monk worthy of esteem has risen in the last watch of the night and is sitting cross-legged, keeping his body erect and establishing mindfulness before him, at that time his body is sustained by essence, and it is pleasant for him to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Therefore, that is not the time to approach a monk worthy of esteem for a visit."

When this was said, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said to the elder monks: "Friends, I have heard and received this from the presence of the Blessed One: 'Monks, there are these six occasions to approach a monk worthy of esteem for a visit.'

What are the six? Here, monks, when a monk dwells with a mind obsessed and oppressed by sensual desire (kāmarāga), and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual desire, at that time he should approach a monk worthy of esteem and say: 'Friend, I dwell with a mind obsessed and oppressed by sensual desire, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual desire. It would be good if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual desire.' The monk worthy of esteem then teaches him the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual desire. Monks, this is the first occasion to approach a monk worthy of esteem for a visit.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk dwells with a mind obsessed and oppressed by ill will (byāpāda)... [as above]... sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha)... restlessness and remorse (uddhaccakukkucca)... doubt (vicikicchā)... Based on whatever sign...
284:
...when he does not know or see that sign, by depending on which and by attending to which the taints (āsavas) are destroyed without delay, at that time he should approach a monk worthy of esteem and say: 'Friend, I do not know or see that sign, by depending on which and by attending to which the taints are destroyed without delay. It would be good if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.' The monk worthy of esteem then teaches him the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints. Monks, this is the sixth occasion to approach a monk worthy of esteem for a visit.

Friends, I have heard and received this from the presence of the Blessed One: 'Monks, these are the six occasions to approach a monk worthy of esteem for a visit.'"

The eighth sutta.

## 9. Udāyī Sutta

29. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyī: "Udāyī, how many bases of mindfulness (anussatiṭṭhāna) are there?" When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī remained silent. A second time the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyī: "Udāyī, how many bases of mindfulness are there?" A second time the Venerable Udāyī remained silent. A third time the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyī: "Udāyī, how many bases of mindfulness are there?" A third time the Venerable Udāyī remained silent.

Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Udāyī: "Friend Udāyī, the Teacher is addressing you."

"Friend Ānanda, I hear the Blessed One. Bhante, here a monk recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... [as above]... Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. Bhante, this is a base of mindfulness."

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "I knew, Ānanda, that this empty man Udāyī does not dwell devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta). Ānanda, how many bases of mindfulness are there?"

"Bhante, there are five bases of mindfulness. What five? Here, Bhante, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above]... enters and dwells in the third jhāna. Bhante, this is a base of mindfulness which, when thus developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

Furthermore, Bhante, a monk attends to the perception of light (ālokasaññā)..."
285:
He attends to the perception of light; as by day, so by night; as by night, so by day. Thus, with an open mind unhindered [by the hindrances], he develops a mind imbued with radiance.

Bhante, this is a base of recollection which, when thus developed and frequently practiced, leads to the acquisition of knowledge and vision (divine eye).

Furthermore, Bhante, a monk reviews this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the tips of the hair downwards, enclosed by skin and full of various kinds of impurities:

'In this body there are: hairs of the head, hairs of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, gorge, dung, (brain), bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine.'

Bhante, this is a base of recollection which, when thus developed and frequently practiced, leads to the abandoning of sensual lust (kāmarāga).

Furthermore, Bhante, as if a monk were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground—one day dead, two days dead, or three days dead, bloated, livid, and festering—he then compares this very body with it: 'This body of mine, too, is of such a nature, will become like that, and is not exempt from that fate.'

Or again, as if he were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, dogs, jackals, or various kinds of worms, he then compares this very body with it: 'This body of mine, too, is of such a nature, will become like that, and is not exempt from that fate.'

Or again, as if he were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by tendons... a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by tendons... a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by tendons... the bones scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, there a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a rib-bone, there a back-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, there a skull—
286:
—seeing the bones white, like the color of a conch shell; seeing the bones piled up, more than a year old; seeing the bones rotted and crumbled into dust, he then compares this very body with it: 'This body of mine, too, is of such a nature, will become like that, and is not exempt from that fate.'

Bhante, this is a base of recollection which, when thus developed and frequently practiced, leads to the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna).

Furthermore, Bhante, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before]... a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Bhante, this is a base of recollection which, when thus developed and frequently practiced, leads to the penetration of many elements (anekadhātu). Bhante, these are the five bases of recollection.

"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! In that case, Ānanda, you should also remember this sixth base of recollection.

Here, Ānanda, a monk mindfully goes forward, mindfully returns, mindfully stands, mindfully sits, mindfully lies down, and mindfully undertakes his work. Ānanda, this is a base of recollection which, when thus developed and frequently practiced, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña)."

Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Anuttariya Sutta

30. "Monks, there are these six supremes. Which six?

The supreme seeing, the supreme hearing, the supreme gain, the supreme training, the supreme service, and the supreme recollection.

And what, monks, is the supreme seeing?

Here, monks, someone goes to see the elephant-treasure, goes to see the horse-treasure, goes to see the jewel-treasure, or goes to see various high and low things, or goes to see a recluse or brahmin of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, that seeing exists; I do not say it does not. But that seeing, monks, is low, vulgar, common, ignoble, and unbeneficial; it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna.

But, monks, whoever goes to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata—"
287:
Monks, when a person, having established faith and established love, having reached unwavering confidence and being fully devoted, goes to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata.

Monks, that going to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata by one who has established faith and established love, who has reached unwavering confidence and is fully devoted—this is the supreme seeing for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.

Monks, this is called the supreme seeing. This is the supreme seeing.

And what, monks, is the supreme hearing?

Monks, in this world, some people go to hear the sound of drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, or various high and low sounds. They also go to hear the teaching of a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and follows a wrong practice. Monks, such hearing exists; I do not say it does not exist. However, monks, that kind of hearing is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna.

Monks, when a person, having established faith and established love, having reached unwavering confidence and being fully devoted, goes to hear the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata.

Monks, that going to hear the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata by one who has established faith and established love, who has reached unwavering confidence and is fully devoted—this is the supreme hearing for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.

Monks, this is called the supreme hearing. This is the supreme seeing and the supreme hearing.

And what, monks, is the supreme gain?

Monks, in this world, some people obtain the gain of a son, the gain of a wife, the gain of wealth, or various high and low gains. They also obtain faith in a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and follows a wrong practice. Monks, such gain exists; I do not say it does not exist. However, monks, that kind of gain is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna.
288:
Monks, when a person, having established faith and established love, having reached unwavering confidence and being fully devoted, obtains faith in the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata.

Monks, that obtaining of faith in the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata by one who has established faith and established love, who has reached unwavering confidence and is fully devoted—this is the supreme gain for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.

Monks, this is called the supreme gain. This is the supreme seeing, the supreme hearing, and the supreme gain.

And what, monks, is the supreme training?

Monks, in this world, some people train in elephant-riding, horse-riding, chariot-driving, or archery. They also train in various high and low arts. They also learn the wrong practice of a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and follows a wrong practice. Monks, such training exists; I do not say it does not exist.

Monks, that kind of training is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna.

Monks, when a person, having established faith and established love, having reached unwavering confidence and being fully devoted, trains in the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

Monks, that training in the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata by one who has established faith and established love, who has reached unwavering confidence and is fully devoted—this is the supreme training for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.

Monks, this is called the supreme training. This is the supreme seeing, the supreme hearing, the supreme gain, and the supreme training.

And what, monks, is the supreme service?

Monks, in this world, some people serve a noble, a brahmin, or a householder. They also serve various high and low persons. They also serve a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and follows a wrong practice. Monks, such service exists; I do not say it does not exist.

Monks, that kind of service is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial. It does not lead to disenchantment... p... or to Nibbāna.
289:
Monks, a person who has established faith and established love, having reached absolute unwavering confidence and being exceedingly devoted, serves the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata.

Monks, whatever service one performs for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, having established faith and established love, having reached absolute unwavering confidence and being exceedingly devoted—this kind of service is the supreme service for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna.

Monks, this service is called the supreme service.

Thus, there are the supreme seeing, the supreme hearing, the supreme gain, the supreme training, and the supreme service.

And how, monks, is there the supreme recollection?

Monks, in this world, some people repeatedly recollect the acquisition of sons, the acquisition of wives, the acquisition of wealth, or they repeatedly recollect various gains, high or low. Or they repeatedly recollect a recluse or a brahmin of wrong view and wrong practice. Monks, such a kind of recollection exists; I do not say it does not exist.

But, monks, this kind of recollection is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna.

Monks, but when one has established faith and established love, having reached absolute unwavering confidence and being exceedingly devoted, one repeatedly recollects the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata.

Monks, whatever repeated recollection one performs for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, having established faith and established love, having reached absolute unwavering confidence and being exceedingly devoted—this kind of recollection is the supreme recollection for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna.

Monks, this recollection is called the supreme recollection.

Monks, these are the six supreme things.

Those who have obtained the supreme seeing, the supreme hearing, and the supreme gain, who delight in the supreme training, and who are established in the supreme service, develop the supreme recollection associated with seclusion, which is peaceful and leads to the Deathless (Nibbāna).
290:
They rejoice in heedfulness, are wise and mature, and are restrained by virtue. In due time, they truly understand the Nibbāna where suffering ceases.

The Tenth Sutta.

The third, Anuttariya-vagga, is finished.

## 4. Devatā-vagga

## 1. Sekha Sutta

31. Monks, these six things lead to the decline of a monk who is a trainee (sekha).

What are the six?

Delight in work.
Delight in talk.
Delight in sleep.
Delight in company.
Not guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
Immoderation in eating.

Monks, these six things lead to the decline of a monk who is a trainee.

Monks, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk who is a trainee.

What are the six?

Not delighting in work.
Not delighting in talk.
Not delighting in sleep.
Not delighting in company.
Guarding the doors of the sense faculties.
Moderation in eating.

Monks, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk who is a trainee.

The First Sutta.

## 2. Paṭhama Aparihāna Sutta

32. Then, when the night was far spent, a certain deity of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk.

What are the six?

Reverence for the Teacher.
Reverence for the Dhamma.
Reverence for the Saṅgha.
Reverence for the training (sikkhā).
Reverence for heedfulness.
Reverence for hospitality (paṭisanthāra)."

"Venerable Sir, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk."

That deity said this, and the Teacher approved. Then that deity, knowing "The Teacher has approved of me," paid homage to the Blessed One and, keeping him on his right, disappeared right there.
291:
Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

“Monks, tonight, a certain deity, as the night was passing, with surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached me, paid homage, and stood to one side. Standing there, monks, that deity said this to me:

‘Venerable sir, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk. Which six?

Reverence for the Teacher (Satthugāravatā),
Reverence for the Dhamma (Dhammagāravatā),
Reverence for the Saṅgha (Saṅghagāravatā),
Reverence for the Training (Sikkhāgāravatā),
Reverence for Heedfulness (Appamādagāravatā),
Reverence for Hospitality (Paṭisanthāragāravatā).

Venerable sir, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk.’

Monks, that deity said this. Having said this, he paid homage to me, and keeping me on his right, disappeared right there.”

“Reverent toward the Teacher and the Dhamma,
And with deep reverence for the Saṅgha;
Reverent toward heedfulness and hospitality,
A monk is incapable of falling away,
He is in the very presence of Nibbāna.”

The second sutta.

## 3. Second Sutta on Non-decline

33. “Monks, tonight, a certain deity, as the night was passing, with surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached me, paid homage, and stood to one side. Standing there, monks, that deity said this to me:

‘Venerable sir, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk. Which six?

Reverence for the Teacher,
Reverence for the Dhamma,
Reverence for the Saṅgha,
Reverence for the Training,
Reverence for Shame (Hirigāravatā),
Reverence for Fear of wrongdoing (Ottappagāravatā).

Venerable sir, these six things lead to the non-decline of a monk.’

Monks, that deity said this. Having said this, he paid homage to me, and keeping me on his right, disappeared right there.”

“Reverent toward the Teacher and the Dhamma,
And with deep reverence for the Saṅgha;
Endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing,
Respectful and reverent,
A monk is incapable of falling away,
He is in the very presence of Nibbāna.”

The third sutta.

## 4. Mahāmoggallāna Sutta

34. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
292:
Then, while Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind:

“Which deities have the knowledge: ‘Those who are Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their destination’?”

At that time, a monk named Tissa had recently passed away and was reborn in a certain Brahma world. There, they knew him as: “Tissa Brahmā is of great power and great majesty.”

Then, just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna disappeared from Jeta’s Grove and appeared in that Brahma world. Tissa Brahmā saw Venerable Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar and said this to him:

“Come, dear Moggallāna! Welcome, dear Moggallāna! It has been a long time, dear Moggallāna, since you have taken the opportunity to come here. Sit down, dear Moggallāna; this seat is prepared.”

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sat on the prepared seat.

Tissa Brahmā also paid homage to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and sat to one side. As Tissa Brahmā was sitting to one side, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to him:

“Tissa, which deities have the knowledge: ‘Those who are Stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their destination’?”

“Dear Moggallāna, the devas of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) have the knowledge: ‘Those who are Stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their destination.’”

“Tissa, do all the devas of the Four Great Kings have the knowledge: ‘Those who are Stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their destination’?”

“Dear Moggallāna, not all the devas of the Four Great Kings have the knowledge: ‘Those who are Stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their destination.’

Dear Moggallāna, those devas of the Four Great Kings who are not endowed with confirmed confidence in the Buddha, not endowed with confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, not endowed with confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha, and not endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, do not have the knowledge: ‘Those who are Stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds...’"
293:
...are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment'—they do not have such knowledge.

"Venerable Moggallāna, those Cātumahārājika devas who possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and who possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, they have such knowledge: 'Stream-enterers are no longer subject to downfall, are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment.'"

"Tissa, does such knowledge—'Stream-enterers are no longer subject to downfall, are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment'—occur only to the Cātumahārājika devas, or also to the Tāvatiṃsa devas... [etc.] ...the Yāma devas... the Tusita devas... the Nimmānarati devas... the Paranimmitavasavatti devas?"

"Venerable sir, such knowledge—'Stream-enterers are no longer subject to downfall, are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment'—occurs also to the Paranimmitavasavatti devas."

"Tissa, does such knowledge—'Stream-enterers are no longer subject to downfall, are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment'—occur to all the Paranimmitavasavatti devas?"

"Venerable Moggallāna, such knowledge—'Stream-enterers are no longer subject to downfall, are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment'—does not occur to all the Paranimmitavasavatti devas.

"Venerable Moggallāna, those Paranimmitavasavatti devas who do not possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and who do not possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, they do not have such knowledge: 'Stream-enterers are no longer subject to downfall, are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment.'

"Venerable Moggallāna, those Paranimmitavasavatti devas who possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and who possess the virtues dear to the noble ones, they have such knowledge: 'Stream-enterers are no longer subject to downfall, are fixed in destiny, and are destined for enlightenment.'"

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having greatly rejoiced in and appreciated the words of Tissa Brahma, just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, even so, he disappeared from the Brahma world and appeared in the Jeta Grove.
294:
Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Vijjābhāgiya Sutta

35. "Bhikkhus, there are these six things that partake of true knowledge. Which six?

The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in the impermanent, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.

Bhikkhus, these six things partake of true knowledge."

Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Vivādamūla Sutta

36. "Bhikkhus, there are these six roots of dispute. Which six?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is angry and resentful. A bhikkhu who is angry and resentful lives without respect or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and he does not fulfill the training.

Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lives without respect or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and who does not fulfill the training, causes dispute in the Saṅgha. That dispute is for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many, of devas and humans.

Bhikkhus, if you should see such a root of dispute either internally or externally, you should strive to abandon that very same evil root of dispute. Bhikkhus, if you should not see such a root of dispute either internally or externally, you should practice so that that very same evil root of dispute does not arise in the future.

When one practices in this way, there is the abandoning of that evil root of dispute. When it is abandoned in this way, that evil root of dispute does not arise in the future.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is contemptuous and domineering... [etc.] ...is envious and stingy... is deceitful and fraudulent... has evil desires and wrong view... adheres to his own views, holds them firmly, and relinquishes them with difficulty.

Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who adheres to his own views, holds them firmly, and relinquishes them with difficulty, lives without respect or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and he does not fulfill the training.

Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who lives without respect or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and who does not fulfill the training, causes dispute in the Saṅgha. That dispute is for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many, of devas and humans."
295:
Monks, if you should see such a root of contention either internally or externally, you should strive to abandon that very evil root of contention. 

Monks, if you should not see such a root of contention either internally or externally, you should practice so that very evil root of contention does not arise in the future. When one practices thus, it is called the abandoning of that evil root of contention. When it is abandoned thus, it is said that the evil root of contention will not arise in the future. Monks, these are the six roots of contention.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Dāna (Chalaṅgadāna) Sutta

37. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. At that time, the laywoman Nandamātā of Veḷukaṇḍaka established an offering endowed with six factors for the Saṅgha of monks headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

The Blessed One saw with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses that of human beings, the laywoman Nandamātā of Veḷukaṇḍaka establishing an offering endowed with six factors for the Saṅgha of monks headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Having seen this, he addressed the monks:

"Monks, this laywoman Nandamātā of Veḷukaṇḍaka is establishing an offering endowed with six factors for the Saṅgha of monks headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

And how, monks, is an offering endowed with six factors?

Monks, in this teaching, there are three factors of the donor and three factors of the recipients.

What are the three factors of the donor?

Monks, in this teaching, the donor is glad before giving, makes the mind clear while giving, and is gratified after giving. These are the three factors of the donor.

What are the three factors of the recipients?

Monks, in this teaching, the recipients are free from lust (rāga), or they are practicing for the removal of lust. They are free from hatred (dosa), or they are practicing for the removal of hatred. They are free from delusion (moha), or they are practicing for the removal of delusion. These are the three factors of the recipients. Thus, there are three factors of the donor and three factors of the recipients. In this way, monks, an offering is endowed with six factors."
296:
"Monks, when an offering is thus endowed with six factors, it is not easy to take the measure of the merit, saying: 'This much is the outflow of merit, the outflow of the wholesome, which brings happiness, provides excellent objects, results in happiness, leads to heaven, and conduces to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.' Rather, it is reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.

Monks, just as in the great ocean it is not easy to take the measure of the water, saying: 'There are this many measures of water,' or 'this many hundreds of measures of water,' or 'this many thousands of measures of water,' or 'this many hundreds of thousands of measures of water,' but rather it is reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water; so too, monks, when an offering is thus endowed with six factors, it is not easy to take the measure of the merit, saying: 'This much is the outflow of merit... [as before] ...and pleasant.' Rather, it is reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.

Glad before giving, with a clear mind while giving,
Gratified after giving: this is the perfection of the sacrifice.
Free from lust, hatred, and delusion, taintless,
Those restrained and living the holy life are the perfect field for the sacrifice.
Having rinsed (the hands, feet, and mouth) oneself, and giving with one's own hands,
That sacrifice, for oneself and for others, is of great fruit in the world beyond.
The wise one of swift wisdom, endowed with faith and a liberated mind,
By giving thus, the sage reaches the happy heavenly world free from suffering."

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Attakārī Sutta

38. Then a certain Brahmin approached the Blessed One and exchanged friendly and courteous greetings with him. After exchanging pleasant and memorable greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that Brahmin said to the Blessed One:

"Master Gotama, I am one who speaks thus: 'There is no self-agency, there is no agency of others.'"
297:
“I am of such a view, I hold such a doctrine: ‘There is no self-agency, there is no other-agency,’” he said.

“Brahmin, I have never seen or heard of anyone holding such a view or such a doctrine. For how can one who himself moves forward and moves backward say: ‘There is no self-agency, there is no other-agency’?

Brahmin, what do you think? Is there an element of initiation (ārabhadhātu)?”
“There is, venerable sir.”
“When there is an element of initiation, are beings who initiate clearly seen?”
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Brahmin, since there is an element of initiation and beings who initiate are clearly seen, this is the self-agency of beings, this is the other-agency.

Brahmin, what do you think? Is there an element of deliverance (nikkamadhātu) [from laziness]? ...
Is there an element of persistence (parakkamadhātu)?
Is there an element of strength (thāmadhātu)?
Is there an element of steadfastness (ṭhitidhātu)?
Is there an element of endeavor (upakkamadhātu)?”
“There is, venerable sir.”
“When there is an element of endeavor, are beings who endeavor clearly seen?”
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Brahmin, since there is an element of endeavor and beings who endeavor are clearly seen, this is the self-agency of beings, this is the other-agency.

Brahmin, I have never seen or heard of anyone holding such a view or such a doctrine. For how can one who himself moves forward and moves backward say: ‘There is no self-agency, there is no other-agency’?”

“Excellent, Master Gotama! ... From this day forth, may Master Gotama regard me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts.”

The eighth sutta.

## 9. Nidāna Sutta
39. “Monks, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma (which lead to the suffering of the round).
What three?
Greed (lobha) is a cause for the origination of kamma.
Hatred (dosa) is a cause for the origination of kamma.
Delusion (moha) is a cause for the origination of kamma.

Monks, non-greed (alobha) does not arise from greed; rather, monks, only greed arises from greed.
Monks, non-hatred (adosa) does not arise from hatred; rather, monks, only hatred arises from hatred.
Monks, non-delusion (amoha) does not arise from delusion; rather, monks, only delusion arises from delusion.

Monks, because of kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, and kamma born of delusion, devas are not seen, humans are not seen, nor are any other happy destinations seen.
Rather, monks, because of kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred...”
298:
“...and kamma born of delusion, hell is seen, the animal realm is seen, the sphere of afflicted spirits is seen, or other unhappy destinations are seen.
Monks, these are the three causes for the origination of kamma (which lead to the suffering of the round).

Monks, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma (which lead to the end of the round, Nibbāna).
What three?
Non-greed (alobha) is a cause for the origination of kamma.
Non-hatred (adosa) is a cause for the origination of kamma.
Non-delusion (amoha) is a cause for the origination of kamma.

Monks, greed (lobha) does not arise from non-greed; rather, monks, only non-greed arises from non-greed.
Monks, hatred (dosa) does not arise from non-hatred; rather, monks, only non-hatred arises from non-hatred.
Monks, delusion (moha) does not arise from non-delusion; rather, monks, only non-delusion arises from non-delusion.

Monks, because of kamma born of non-greed, kamma born of non-hatred, and kamma born of non-delusion, hell is not seen, the animal realm is not seen, the sphere of afflicted spirits is not seen, nor are any other unhappy destinations seen.
Rather, monks, because of kamma born of non-greed, kamma born of non-hatred, and kamma born of non-delusion, devas are seen, humans are seen, and other happy destinations and states of existence are seen.
Monks, these are the three causes for the origination of kamma (which lead to the end of the round, Nibbāna).”

The ninth sutta.

## 10. Kimila Sutta
40. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kimilā in the Bamboo Grove.
Then the venerable Kimila approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the venerable Kimila said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the True Dhamma does not last long after the Tathāgata has attained parinibbāna?”

“Kimila, when the Tathāgata has attained parinibbāna, if the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen:
Dwell without respect and without deference toward the Teacher.
Dwell without respect and without deference toward the Dhamma.
Dwell without respect and without deference toward the Saṅgha.
Dwell without respect and without deference toward the Training (sikkhā).
Dwell without respect and without deference toward Heedfulness (appamāda).
Dwell without respect and without deference toward Hospitality (paṭisanthāra).
Kimila, this is the cause, this is the reason, why the True Dhamma does not last long after the Tathāgata has attained parinibbāna.”

“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the True Dhamma lasts long after the Tathāgata has attained parinibbāna?”
299:
And what is the cause, what is the condition? (he asked).

Kimila, in this Dispensation, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen:
Dwell with respect and deference toward the Teacher.
Dwell with respect and deference toward the Dhamma.
Dwell with respect and deference toward the Saṅgha.
Dwell with respect and deference toward the Training (Sikkhā).
Dwell with respect and deference toward Heedfulness (Appamāda).
Dwell with respect and deference toward Hospitality (Paṭisanthāra).

Kimila, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, this is the cause, this is the condition, by which the True Dhamma lasts for a long time. (the Blessed One said).

The tenth sutta.

## 11. Dārukkhandha Sutta

41. Thus have I heard—
At one time, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Rājagaha, on the Gijjhakūṭa Hill.

Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and while descending from Gijjhakūṭa Hill with a large number of monks, he saw a large log in a certain place. Seeing it, he addressed the monks:

“Friends, do you see this large log?”

“Yes, friend,” they replied.

“Friends, if he so desired, a monk who is possessed of psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind could resolve this large log to be only earth. Why is that?

Friends, the earth element (pathavīdhātu) exists in this large log, depending on which a monk who is possessed of psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind could resolve this large log to be only earth.

Friends, if he so desired, a monk who is possessed of psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind could resolve this large log to be only water. [p]
To be only fire.
To be only air.
To be only beautiful.
To be only foul. Why is that?

Friends, the foul element (asubhadhātu) exists in this large log, depending on which a monk who is possessed of psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind could resolve this large log to be only foul.” (he said).

The eleventh sutta.

## 12. Nāgita Sutta

42. Thus have I heard—
At one time, the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala.
300:
The Blessed One stayed in the Icchānaṅgala wood near the village of Icchānaṅgala. The brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard the news:

“Friends, it is said that the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is staying in the Icchānaṅgala wood near Icchānaṅgala. A good reputation concerning that Blessed Gotama has spread thus:

‘That Blessed One is an Arahant because he is worthy of special offerings; he is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) because he has rightly understood all things by himself; he is endowed with knowledge (Vijjā) and conduct (Caraṇa). [p] He is the Buddha because he makes others understand the Four Noble Truths; he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he possesses great glory.’ (Thus it spread). That Blessed Gotama has realized for himself this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās... [p] It is good to see such Arahants.” (Thus they heard).

Then, when the night had passed, the brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala took many kinds of food and snacks and went to the Icchānaṅgala wood. They stood outside the gatehouse making a loud noise, a great uproar. At that time, the Venerable Nāgita was the Blessed One’s attendant. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Nāgita: “Nāgita, who are those making such a loud noise, such a great uproar, like fishermen at a haul of fish?”

“Venerable Sir, these are the brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala. They are standing outside the gatehouse with many kinds of food and snacks, intended for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks.”

“Nāgita, may I not be joined with fame, and may fame not be joined with me.

Nāgita, for one who cannot obtain at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, this bliss of renunciation (nekkhamma), this bliss of seclusion (paviveka), this bliss of peace (upasama), this bliss of enlightenment (sambodha)—let him enjoy that bliss of filth, that bliss of sloth, that bliss of gain, honor, and fame.

But for me, who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, this bliss of renunciation, this bliss of seclusion, this bliss of peace, and this bliss of enlightenment, how could I enjoy that bliss of filth, that bliss of sloth, and that bliss of gain, honor, and fame?” (the Blessed One said).

“Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One accept now; let the Sugata accept now. Now is the time for the Blessed One to accept. Venerable Sir, in whatever direction the Blessed One goes now, the brahmins and householders, the townspeople and countryfolk, will lean in that same direction. Just as, Venerable Sir, when it rains in thick drops, the water flows downhill, even so, in whatever direction the Blessed One goes now, the brahmins and householders, the townspeople and countryfolk, will lean in that same direction. Why is that? Because of the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.”

“Nāgita, may I not be joined with fame, and may fame not be joined with me. Nāgita, for one who cannot obtain at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, this bliss of renunciation, this bliss of seclusion, this bliss of peace...”
301:
“Venerable Sir, now is the time for the Blessed One to be forbearing. Venerable Sir, now is the time for the Blessed One to be forbearing. Wherever the Blessed One may go, the brahmins and householders of the market towns and the countryside will be inclined to follow him. Venerable Sir, just as when it rains heavily, the water flows down to the low-lying areas, in the same way, Venerable Sir, wherever the Blessed One may go, the brahmins and householders of the market towns and the countryside will be inclined to follow him. For what reason is that?

Venerable Sir, it is because the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom are so great.” (Nagita said.)

“Nagita, I do not wish to be associated with fame, nor let fame be associated with me. Nagita, whoever cannot obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, this bliss of renunciation (nekkhamma), this bliss of seclusion (paviveka), this bliss of peace (upasama), and this bliss of enlightenment (sambodha), let him enjoy that filthy pleasure, that pleasure of sloth, and that pleasure of gain, honor, and fame.

Nagita, since I can obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, this bliss of renunciation, this bliss of seclusion, this bliss of peace, and this bliss of enlightenment, why should I enjoy that filthy pleasure, that pleasure of sloth, and that pleasure of gain, honor, and fame?

Nagita, here in this Dispensation, I see a village-dwelling monk sitting in concentration. To me, Nagita, the thought occurs: ‘Now, either a monastery attendant or a novice will disturb this venerable one and cause him to fall away from that concentration.’ Therefore, Nagita, I am not pleased with that monk’s village-dwelling.

Nagita, here in this Dispensation, I see a forest-dwelling monk sitting in the forest nodding in sleep. To me, Nagita, the thought occurs: ‘Now, this venerable one, having dispelled this fatigue from sleep, will attend only to the perception of the forest, which is a state of oneness.’ Therefore, Nagita, I am pleased with that monk’s forest-dwelling.

Nagita, here in this Dispensation, I see a forest-dwelling monk sitting in the forest without concentration. To me, Nagita, the thought occurs:
‘Now, this venerable one will either concentrate his unconcentrated mind or protect his concentrated mind.’
Therefore, Nagita, I am pleased with that monk’s forest-dwelling.

Nagita, here in this Dispensation, I see a forest-dwelling monk sitting in the forest in concentration. To me, Nagita, the thought occurs:
‘Now, this venerable one will either liberate his unliberated mind or protect his liberated mind.’
302:
“Therefore, Nagita, I am pleased with that monk’s forest-dwelling.

Nagita, here in this Dispensation, I see a village-dwelling monk who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Desiring that gain, honor, and fame, he abandons solitary seclusion and abandons remote lodgings in the forest and jungle; he enters and dwells in villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Therefore, Nagita, I am not pleased with that monk’s village-dwelling.

Nagita, here in this Dispensation, I see a forest-dwelling monk who receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Having set aside that gain, honor, and fame, he does not abandon solitary seclusion and does not abandon remote lodgings in the forest and jungle. Therefore, Nagita, I am pleased with that monk’s forest-dwelling.

Nagita, when I am traveling along a highway and see no one either in front of me or behind me, at that time I am at ease, even in regard to the discharge of excrement and urine.” (The Blessed One said.)

The twelfth sutta.
The fourth Devatā Vagga is finished.

## 5. Dhammika Vagga
## 1. Nāga Sutta

43. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on his return from the alms round, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern Monastery, the mansion of Migāramātā (Visākhā), for the day’s abiding.”

“Yes, Venerable Sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the Eastern Monastery, the mansion of Migāramātā.

Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his solitary seclusion and addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern Bathing Place to bathe our limbs.”

“Yes, Venerable Sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the Eastern Bathing Place to bathe his limbs.
303:
Having bathed his limbs at the eastern bathing place (Pubbakoṭṭhaka), he emerged and stood clad in a single robe, letting his limbs dry. 

At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala's elephant named Seta emerged from the eastern bathing place to the sound of a great musical performance. Seeing that royal white elephant, the people said: 

"Friends, the King's elephant is truly handsome! Friends, the King's elephant is truly a sight to behold! Friends, the King's elephant is truly pleasing! Friends, the King's elephant is truly possessed of a majestic body!"

When this was said, the Venerable Kāḷudāyī said to the Blessed One: 

"Venerable Sir, do people say 'Friends, a Nāga indeed! A Nāga indeed!' only when they see a large, majestic elephant possessed of a majestic body? Or do they say 'Friends, a Nāga indeed! A Nāga indeed!' when they see any other large, majestic being?"

"Udāyī, people say 'Friends, a Nāga indeed! A Nāga indeed!' when they see a large, majestic elephant possessed of a majestic body. 

Udāyī, [they say the same] when they see a large, majestic horse... 

Udāyī, [they say the same] when they see a large, majestic bull... 

Udāyī, [they say the same] when they see a large, majestic snake... 

Udāyī, [they say the same] when they see a large, majestic tree with a majestic trunk... 

Udāyī, people say 'Friends, a Nāga indeed! A Nāga indeed!' when they see a large, majestic human possessed of a majestic body. 

However, Udāyī, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and people, I call one who does no evil by body, speech, or mind a 'Nāga'."

"It is wonderful, Venerable Sir! It is amazing, Venerable Sir! How well-spoken this is by the Blessed One: 'However, Udāyī, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and people, I call one who does no evil by body, speech, or mind a Nāga.' 

Venerable Sir, I rejoice in these well-spoken words of the Blessed One with these verses: 

'The people worship that Blessed One who is a true human, self-tamed and concentrated, walking on the noble path, delighting in the stillness of the mind (the fourth jhāna), who has reached the further shore of all dhammas. I have heard from the Blessed One, who is worthy of offerings, that even the devas worship him who has transcended all fetters, who has come out of the forest (of defilements) to the forestless state, who delights in renunciation from sensual pleasures, and who is like pure gold freed from dross. Just as Mount Himavanta shines surpassing other mountains, so too the Blessed One is the Nāga who shines surpassing all others.'"
304:
## 
"Among all those named 'Nāga', the peerless Buddha is the one truly named 'Nāga'. I shall proclaim the reason for your name 'Nāga', for that Blessed One does no evil. Gentleness and non-harming (avihimsā) are the two front feet of the Nāga-like Lord. 

Austerity and the holy life (the noble path) are the other two back feet of the Nāga-like Lord. The Great Nāga has faith as his trunk, and the six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) as his white tusks. Mindfulness is his neck. 

Omniscience is his head. The wisdom that contemplates the Dhamma is the tip of his trunk. The Dhamma (the concentration of the fourth jhāna) is his belly. The three kinds of seclusion (viveka) are the tail-hair of that Nāga-like Buddha. 

He is a meditator, delighting in the breath (fruition attainment), with a mind well-composed within. Walking, the Buddha-Nāga is well-composed; standing, the Buddha-Nāga is well-composed. 

Lying down, the Buddha-Nāga is well-composed; sitting, the Buddha-Nāga is well-composed. Everywhere the Buddha-Nāga is well-restrained; this is the perfection of the Nāga. 

He consumes blameless requisites and does not consume blameworthy ones. Having obtained food and clothing, he avoids hoarding them. 

Having cut all fetters, small and large, he goes wherever he wishes, without looking back. 

Just as a white lotus (puṇḍarīka), born in the water, grows in the water, and is not defiled by the water, being of pure fragrance and delightful; 

So too the Buddha, well-born in the world, dwells in the world, but is not defiled by the world, just as the lotus is not defiled by the water."
305:
“Just as a lotus is not smeared by water, so he is not smeared or attached to the world. Just as a great blazing fire is extinguished when there is no fuel, so when formations (saṅkhāra) cease, he is said to be extinguished. This simile, which conveys the meaning, is taught by the wise. The great elephants (Arahants) will understand the Elephant (the Buddha) taught by the elephant-like Kāḷudāyī. Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, and without taints (āsava), the Naga (the Buddha), abandoning the body, being free from taints, will attain Parinibbāna.” (Thus he praised.)

First Sutta.

## 2. Migasālā Sutta

44. Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the residence of the laywoman Migasālā and sat on the prepared seat. Then the laywoman Migasālā approached the Venerable Ānanda, paid homage to him, and sat to one side. Sitting there, the laywoman Migasālā said to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how should this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One be understood? For in this Dhamma, both a celibate (brahmacārī) and a non-celibate (abrahmacārī) have the same destination (gati) in the next life. Venerable sir, my father named Purāṇa was a celibate; he lived apart and abstained from sexual intercourse, the village-dharma. When my father passed away, the Blessed One declared: ‘Having attained the fruit of Once-returner (sakadāgāmī), he is reborn in the Tusita heaven.’

Venerable sir, my uncle named Isidatta was a non-celibate, being content with his own wife. When he also passed away, the Blessed One declared: ‘Having attained the fruit of Once-returner, he is reborn in the Tusita heaven.’

Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how should this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One be understood? For in this Dhamma, both a celibate and a non-celibate have the same destination in the next life.”

“Sister, it was indeed declared so by the Blessed One.”

Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having received alms at the house of the laywoman Migasālā, rose from his seat and departed. After the meal, having returned from the alms-round, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat to one side. He then addressed the Blessed One with these words:
306:
“Venerable sir, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I approached the residence of the laywoman Migasālā and sat on the prepared seat. Then the laywoman Migasālā approached me, paid homage to me, and sat to one side. Sitting there, the laywoman Migasālā said to me:

‘Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how should this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One be understood? For in this Dhamma, both a celibate and a non-celibate have the same destination (gati) in the next life. Venerable sir, my father named Purāṇa was a celibate; he lived apart and abstained from sexual intercourse, the village-dharma. When my father passed away, the Blessed One declared: “Having attained the fruit of Once-returner, he is reborn in the Tusita heaven.”

Venerable sir, my uncle named Isidatta was a non-celibate, being content with his own wife. When he also passed away, the Blessed One declared: “Having attained the fruit of Once-returner, he is reborn in the Tusita heaven.”

Venerable Ānanda, in what way and how should this Dhamma taught by the Blessed One be understood? For in this Dhamma, both a celibate and a non-celibate have the same destination in the next life.’

Venerable sir, when she said this, I told the laywoman Migasālā: ‘Sister, it was indeed declared so by the Blessed One.’

“Ānanda, who is this laywoman Migasālā, a foolish, incompetent woman, a mere woman with a woman’s perception? And who are those (the Buddhas) who have no obstruction in the knowledge of the degree of others’ faculties (indriyaparopariyañāṇa)?

Ānanda, these six types of persons are found existing in the world.

What six?

Ānanda, here in this world, a certain person is gentle and pleasant to live with; his fellow celibates delight in living with him. But he has not done what should be done through hearing, nor through much learning (effort), nor has he penetrated it with wisdom, nor does he attain temporary liberation (vimutti). With the breaking up of the body, after death, he is headed for decline, not for excellence; he goes to decline, not to excellence. (1)

Ānanda, here in this world, a certain person is gentle and pleasant to live with; his fellow celibates delight in living with him. But he has done what should be done through hearing, through much learning (effort), and has penetrated it with wisdom...”
307:
...he also attains temporary liberation (vimutti). After the breaking up of the body, after death, he is headed for distinction, not for decline; he goes to distinction, not to decline. (2)

Ananda, in this case, those who measure persons measure thus: 'This person has these same qualities, and the other person also has these same qualities. Why then is one of them inferior and the other superior?' Ananda, such measuring leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.

Ananda, among these two persons, the one who is gentle, pleasant to live with, whose fellow practitioners delight in living with him, who has practiced by listening, who has practiced by great learning, who has penetrated with wisdom, and who attains temporary liberation—this person is more excellent and more refined than the former person. Why is that? Ananda, the stream of Dhamma carries this person along. Who else can know this difference except the Tathāgata?

Therefore, Ananda, do not be measurers of persons; do not take the measure of persons. Ananda, one who takes the measure of persons digs himself up. Ananda, I, or one like me, may take the measure of persons.

Ananda, here some person is overcome by anger and pride, and from time to time, states of greed arise in him. He has not practiced by listening, has not practiced by great learning, has not penetrated with wisdom, and does not attain temporary liberation. After the breaking up of the body, after death, he is headed for decline, not for distinction; he goes to decline, not to distinction. (3)

Ananda, here some person is overcome by anger and pride, and from time to time, states of greed arise in him. But he has practiced by listening... [as above] ...he goes to distinction, not to decline. (4)

Ananda, in this case, those who measure persons... [as above] ...or one like me, may take the measure of persons.
308:
Ananda, here some person is overcome by anger and pride, and from time to time, verbal formations (vaci-saṅkhāra) arise in him. He has not practiced by listening... [as above] ...does not attain temporary liberation. After the breaking up of the body, after death, he is headed for decline, not for distinction; he goes to decline, not to distinction. (5)

Ananda, here some person is overcome by anger and pride, and from time to time, verbal formations arise in him. But he has practiced by listening, has practiced by great learning, has penetrated with wisdom, and attains temporary liberation. After the breaking up of the body, after death, he is headed for distinction, not for decline; he goes to distinction, not to decline. (6)

Ananda, in this case, those who measure persons measure thus: 'This person has these same qualities, and the other person also has these same qualities. Why then is one of them inferior and the other superior?' Ananda, such measuring leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.

Ananda, among these two persons, the one who is overcome by anger and pride, in whom verbal formations arise from time to time, but who has practiced by listening, has practiced by great learning, has penetrated with wisdom, and attains temporary liberation—this person is more excellent and more refined than the former person. Why is that? Ananda, the stream of Dhamma carries this person along. Who else can know this difference except the Tathāgata?

Therefore, Ananda, do not be measurers of persons; do not take the measure of persons. Ananda, one who takes the measure of persons digs himself up. Ananda, I, or one like me, may take the measure of persons.

Ananda, who is the laywoman Migasālā—foolish, incompetent, a mere woman with a woman’s understanding—and who is the knowledge of the degree of faculties of other persons (indriya-paropariya-ñāṇa)? [Only the Buddhas have such unobstructed knowledge].

Ananda, these six types of persons are found existing in the world.

Ananda, if Isidatta were endowed with the same kind of virtue as Purāṇa was, then Purāṇa would not have known even the destination of Isidatta. And if Purāṇa were endowed with the same kind of wisdom as Isidatta was...
309:
“Ānanda, if Purāṇa were endowed with the same kind of perfected wisdom as Isidatta, Isidatta would not have known Purāṇa’s destination. Ānanda, thus these two persons were each deficient in one factor.”

Second Sutta.

1. Purāṇa excelled in virtue; Isidatta excelled in wisdom. Purāṇa’s virtue was established in the sphere of Isidatta’s wisdom, and Isidatta’s wisdom was established in the sphere of Purāṇa’s virtue. Therefore, they both attained rebirth in the Tusita heaven (Commentary).

## 3. Ina Sutta

45. “Monks, is poverty a suffering for one who enjoys sensual pleasures in the world?” — “Yes, Bhante.”

“Monks, when a poor, destitute, and indigent person takes a loan, is the taking of a loan also a suffering for one who enjoys sensual pleasures in the world?” — “Yes, Bhante.”

“Monks, when a poor, destitute, and indigent person, having taken a loan, agrees to pay interest, is the agreement to pay interest also a suffering for one who enjoys sensual pleasures in the world?” — “Yes, Bhante.”

“Monks, when a poor, destitute, and indigent person, having agreed to pay interest, cannot pay the interest when it is due, and the creditors dun him; is being dunned also a suffering for one who enjoys sensual pleasures in the world?” — “Yes, Bhante.”

“Monks, when a poor, destitute, and indigent person, being dunned, does not pay, and the creditors pursue him; is being pursued also a suffering for one who enjoys sensual pleasures in the world?” — “Yes, Bhante.”

“Monks, when a poor, destitute, and indigent person, being pursued, does not pay, and the creditors bind him; is being bound also a suffering for one who enjoys sensual pleasures in the world?” — “Yes, Bhante.”

“Thus, monks, poverty is suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures, taking a loan is suffering, interest is suffering, being dunned is suffering, being pursued is suffering, and being bound is suffering.

In the same way, monks, for anyone who has no faith in wholesome states, no shame (hiri) in wholesome states, no fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) in wholesome states, no energy (vīriya) in wholesome states, and no wisdom (paññā) in wholesome states—this person is called poor, destitute, and indigent in the discipline of the Noble Ones.

Monks, when that poor, destitute, and indigent person has no faith, no shame, no fear of wrongdoing, no energy, and no wisdom in wholesome states, he practices misconduct by body, speech, and mind. This, I say, is his taking of a loan. For the sake of concealing that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, he harbors evil desires. He desires, ‘May others not know me.’
310:
He thinks, ‘May others not know me’; he speaks, ‘May others not know me’; he makes physical effort, ‘May others not know me.’ This, I say, is his accumulation of interest.

Fellow practitioners who are virtuous say of him: ‘This venerable one acts in such a way, behaves in such a way.’ This, I say, is his being dunned.

When he has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, evil unwholesome thoughts accompanied by remorse beset him. This, I say, is his being pursued.

Monks, that poor, destitute, indigent person, having practiced misconduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, is bound in the bond of hell or the bond of the animal realm.

Monks, I do not see any other single bond so cruel, so bitter, and so obstructive to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage (Nibbāna) as this bond of hell or the bond of the animal realm.

“Poverty is called suffering in the world, and so is the taking of a loan.
A poor man, having taken a loan, suffers while consuming it.

Then they pursue him, and he also meets with imprisonment.
For those who long for the gain of sensual pleasures, that imprisonment is indeed suffering.

In the same way, in the discipline of the Noble Ones, one who has no faith,
Who is shameless and fearless of wrongdoing, accumulates evil deeds.

Having practiced bodily misconduct, and verbal misconducts,
And having practiced mental misconduct, he desires: ‘May others not know me.’

One who increases misconduct by body, speech, and mind,
Constantly wavers and trembles in that evil.
That poor person of evil deeds and no wisdom, knowing his own bad conduct,
Suffers while consuming (his life) as if he had taken a loan.

Because of that consumption of debt, thoughts of remorse that cause mental suffering
Pursue him whether he is in the village or in the forest.”
311:
That foolish person of evil deeds, knowing his own misconduct, having gone to some [animal] womb or to hell, is bound. This is indeed a painful bond, from which the wise man is freed, gladdening the mind by giving with wealth acquired righteously. For the faithful house-seeker, there is a winning throw in both worlds: for the benefit in the present life and for happiness in the future life. Thus, for these householders, the merit of generosity increases. 

Just so, in the Noble One's Discipline, one in whom faith is established, who is conscientious and fearful of wrongdoing, wise and restrained by virtue—he is called one who lives happily in the Noble One's Discipline. Having abandoned the five hindrances, constantly energetic, having entered upon the jhānas, unified in mind, prudent, and mindful, he attains a non-material happiness and abides firmly in equanimity (the fourth jhāna). 

Knowing thus as it really is, in the destruction of all fetters, without clinging in any way, the mind is rightly liberated. For that person who is rightly liberated and endowed with equanimity, if the knowledge of reviewing arises: 'My liberation is unshakable,' then in the destruction of the fetters of existence, this knowledge is supreme. This happiness is called sorrowless, stainless, secure, and unsurpassed; this knowledge is supreme, being free from the debt of defilements.
312:
Third Sutta.

## 4. Mahācunda Sutta

46. Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Venerable Mahācunda was staying among the Cetis at Sahajāti. There the Venerable Mahācunda addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus!" "Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahācunda. The Venerable Mahācunda said this:

"Friends, here those bhikkhus who are devoted to the Dhamma disparage those bhikkhus who are meditators, saying: 'These bhikkhus say, "We are meditators, we are meditators," and they meditate, they over-meditate, they out-meditate, they down-meditate. What do they meditate on? For what purpose do they meditate? How do they meditate?' In that case, neither the bhikkhus devoted to the Dhamma are pleased, nor are the meditator bhikkhus pleased; and they do not practice for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, for the good, welfare, and happiness of many people, of devas and humans.

"Furthermore, friends, here those bhikkhus who are meditators disparage those bhikkhus who are devoted to the Dhamma, saying: 'These bhikkhus say, "We are devoted to the Dhamma, we are devoted to the Dhamma," but they are restless, puffed up, fickle, talkative, loose-tongued, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds and unrestrained faculties. How do they practice Dhamma-devotion? For what purpose do they practice Dhamma-devotion? How do they practice Dhamma-devotion?' In that case, neither the meditator bhikkhus are pleased, nor are the bhikkhus devoted to the Dhamma pleased; and they do not practice for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, for the good, welfare, and happiness of many people, of devas and humans.

"Furthermore, friends, here those bhikkhus who are devoted to the Dhamma speak only in praise of those bhikkhus who are devoted to the Dhamma, and not in praise of those bhikkhus who are meditators. In that case, neither the bhikkhus devoted to the Dhamma are pleased, nor are the meditator bhikkhus pleased; and they do not practice for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, for the good, welfare, and happiness of many people, of devas and humans.

"Furthermore, friends, here those bhikkhus who are meditators speak only in praise of those bhikkhus who are meditators, and not in praise of those bhikkhus who are devoted to the Dhamma. In that case, neither the meditator bhikkhus are pleased, nor are the bhikkhus devoted to the Dhamma pleased;"
313:
They do not practice for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, for the benefit of the many, for the welfare and happiness of devas and humans.

Therefore, friends, you should train yourselves thus: 'When there are monks who are Dhamma-devotees, we will speak in praise of the monks who are meditators.' Thus, friends, should you train yourselves.

Why is that?

Because those persons who dwell having touched the deathless element (Nibbāna) with the mental body are wonderful and rare in the world.

Therefore, friends, you should train yourselves thus: 'When there are monks who are meditators, we will speak in praise of the monks who are Dhamma-devotees.' Thus, friends, should you train yourselves.

Why is that?

Because those persons who see by penetrating with wisdom the profound meaning (the groups of aggregates, sense bases, and elements) are wonderful and rare in the world.

The Fourth Discourse.

## 5. Paṭhama Sandiṭṭhika Sutta

47. Then the wanderer Moliyasīvaka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Moliyasīvaka said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, it is said, 'The Dhamma is visible here and now, the Dhamma is visible here and now.' In what way, venerable sir, is the Dhamma visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, applicable, and to be personally realized by the wise?"

"In that case, Sīvaka, I will question you in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Sīvaka? When greed is present within you, do you know, 'Greed is present within me'? And when greed is not present within you, do you know, 'Greed is not present within me'?"

"Yes, venerable sir."

"Sīvaka, when you know greed present within you as 'Greed is present within me,' and greed not present within you as 'Greed is not present within me,' in this way, Sīvaka, the Dhamma is visible here and now... (p) ...

What do you think, Sīvaka? When hatred (dosa) is present within you... (p) ... When delusion (moha) is present within you... (p) ... When a state associated with greed is present within you... (p) ... When a state associated with hatred is present within you... (p) ... When a state associated with delusion is present within you, do you know, 'A state associated with delusion is present within me'? And when a state associated with delusion is not present within you, do you know, 'A state associated with delusion is not present within me'?"
314:
"Yes, venerable sir."

"Sīvaka, when you know a state associated with delusion present within you as 'A state associated with delusion is present within me,' and a state associated with delusion not present within you as 'A state associated with delusion is not present within me,' in this way, Sīvaka, the Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, applicable, and to be personally realized by the wise."

"Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! ... (p) ... May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The Fifth Discourse.

## 6. Dutiya Sandiṭṭhika Sutta

48. Then a certain Brahmin approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that Brahmin said to the Blessed One:
