"In that case, Brahmin, I will question you in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Brahmin? When lust (rāga) is present within you, do you know, 'Lust is present within me'? And when lust is not present within you, do you know, 'Lust is not present within me'?"

"Yes, Master Gotama."

"Brahmin, when you know lust present within you as 'Lust is present within me,' and lust not present within you as 'Lust is not present within me,' in this way, Brahmin, the Dhamma is visible here and now... (p) ...

What do you think, Brahmin? When hatred (dosa) is present within you... (p) ... When delusion (moha) is present within you... (p) ... When bodily corruption (kāyasandosa) is present within you... (p) ... When verbal corruption (vacīsandosa) is present within you... (p) ... When mental corruption (manosandosa) is present within you, do you know, 'Mental corruption is present within me'? And when mental corruption is not present within you, do you know, 'Mental corruption is not present within me'?"

"Yes, Master Gotama."

"Brahmin, when you know mental corruption present within you as 'Mental corruption is present within me,' and mental corruption not present within you as 'Mental corruption is not present within me,' in this way, Brahmin, the Dhamma is visible here and now,"
315:
It gives results without delay; it is inviting one to come and see; it is worthy of being brought into one's own heart; it is to be realized by the wise, each for himself.

"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Khema Sutta

49. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery.

At that time, the Venerable Khema and the Venerable Sumana were staying at Sāvatthī in the Andhavana Forest. Then the Venerable Khema and the Venerable Sumana approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down at one side. Sitting at one side, the Venerable Khema said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, the thought does not occur: 'I am superior,' or 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.'"

This is what the Venerable Khema said. The Teacher approved. Then the Venerable Khema, knowing that the Teacher approved, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed.

Then, not long after the Venerable Khema had left, the Venerable Sumana said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, the thought does not occur: 'I am not superior,' or 'I am not equal,' or 'I am not inferior.'"

This is what the Venerable Sumana said. The Teacher approved. Then the Venerable Sumana, knowing that the Teacher approved, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed.

Then, not long after the Venerable Khema and the Venerable Sumana had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

"Bhikkhus, it is in this way that clansmen declare their final knowledge. The meaning is stated, but the self is not brought forward.
316:
Yet, there are some hollow men here who declare final knowledge as if in jest; they later meet with distress."

"Not among the superior, nor the inferior,
Nor among the equals are they to be found.
Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived;
They wander free from fetters."

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Indriyasaṃvara Sutta

50. "Bhikkhus, when there is no restraint of the sense faculties, for one who lacks sense restraint, virtue has its proximate cause destroyed. When there is no virtue, for one who lacks virtue, right concentration has its proximate cause destroyed. When there is no right concentration, for one who lacks right concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they are has its proximate cause destroyed. When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they are, for one who lacks knowledge and vision of things as they are, disenchantment and dispassion have their proximate cause destroyed. When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one who lacks disenchantment and dispassion, knowledge and vision of liberation has its proximate cause destroyed.

Just as, bhikkhus, when a tree lacks branches and foliage, its shoots do not reach fullness, its bark does not reach fullness, its softwood does not reach fullness, and its heartwood does not reach fullness; in the same way, bhikkhus, when there is no restraint of the sense faculties, for one who lacks sense restraint, virtue has its proximate cause destroyed. ... knowledge and vision of liberation has its proximate cause destroyed.

Bhikkhus, when there is restraint of the sense faculties, for one who possesses sense restraint, virtue has its proximate cause fulfilled. When there is virtue, for one who possesses virtue, right concentration has its proximate cause fulfilled. When there is right concentration, for one who possesses right concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they are has its proximate cause fulfilled. When there is knowledge and vision of things as they are, for one who possesses knowledge and vision of things as they are, disenchantment and dispassion have their proximate cause fulfilled. When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one who possesses disenchantment and dispassion, knowledge and vision of liberation has its proximate cause fulfilled.

Just as, bhikkhus, when a tree possesses branches and foliage, its shoots reach fullness, its bark reaches fullness, its softwood reaches fullness, and its heartwood reaches fullness; in the same way,
317:
“Monks, in just the same way, when there is restraint of the sense faculties, for a monk who is accomplished in restraint of the sense faculties, virtue (restraint of the Pātimokkha) has its proximate cause for fulfillment... [pe]... the knowledge and vision of liberation (the fruit of Arahatship) and the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) that reflects upon it have their proximate cause for fulfillment.”

The eighth sutta.

## 9. Ānanda Sutta

51. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“Friend Sāriputta, by how much is a monk one who hears the Dhamma not heard before, and the teachings he has heard do not go to forgetfulness, and those teachings that were previously contacted by his mind occur to him, and he understands what was not known before?”

“The Venerable Ānanda is very learned. Let it occur to the Venerable Ānanda himself [to answer this].”

“Then, friend Sāriputta, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.”

“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this:

“Here, friend Sāriputta, a monk learns the Dhamma—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. He teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it; he makes others recite the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it; he chants the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it; he ponders, examines, and inspects the Dhamma with his mind as he has heard and learned it. He enters the rains residence in a monastery where elder monks reside who are very learned, masters of the tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā. He approaches those elders from time to time and asks: ‘How is this, Bhante? What is the meaning of this?’ Those elders reveal to him what was not revealed, clarify what was not clear, and dispel his doubts regarding various points of the Dhamma.

By this much, friend Sāriputta, a monk hears the Dhamma not heard before, and the teachings he has heard do not go to forgetfulness, and those teachings that were previously contacted by his mind occur to him, and he understands what was not known before.”
318:
“...and he understands what was not known before.”

“It is wonderful, friend Ānanda! It is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How well this was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda. We regard the Venerable Ānanda as one endowed with these six qualities:

The Venerable Ānanda learns the Dhamma—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla.

The Venerable Ānanda teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it.

The Venerable Ānanda makes others recite the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it.

The Venerable Ānanda chants the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it.

The Venerable Ānanda ponders, examines, and inspects the Dhamma with his mind as he has heard and learned it.

The Venerable Ānanda enters the rains residence in a monastery where elder monks reside who are very learned, masters of the tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā. The Venerable Ānanda approaches those elders from time to time and asks: ‘How is this, Bhante? What is the meaning of this?’ Those elders reveal to the Venerable Ānanda what was not revealed, clarify what was not clear, and dispel his doubts regarding various points of the Dhamma.”

The ninth sutta.

## 10. Khattiya Sutta

52. Then the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, what is the aim of the Khattiyas? What is their pursuit? What is their support? What is their obsession? What is their final goal?”

“Brahmin, the Khattiyas have wealth as their aim, wisdom as their pursuit, power as their support, territory as their obsession, and sovereignty as their final goal.”

“Master Gotama, what is the aim of the Brahmins? What is their pursuit? What is their support? What is their obsession? What is their final goal?”

“Brahmin, the Brahmins have wealth as their aim, wisdom as their pursuit, mantras as their support, sacrifice as their obsession, and the Brahma world as their final goal.”

“Master Gotama, what is the aim of the householders?...”
319:
“What is their aim? What is their preoccupation? What is their support? What is their resolve? What is their end?” (he asked).

“Brahmin, householders aim for wealth, are preoccupied with wisdom, their support is their craft, their resolve is their work, and their end is finished work,” (the Buddha replied).

“But Master Gotama, what is the aim of women? What is their preoccupation? What is their support? What is their resolve? What is their end?”

“Brahmin, women aim for men, are preoccupied with adornment, their support is their sons, their resolve is being without a co-wife, and their end is authority.”

“But Master Gotama, what is the aim of thieves? What is their preoccupation? What is their support? What is their resolve? What is their end?”

“Brahmin, thieves aim for taking (what is not given), are preoccupied with hiding, their support is weapons, their resolve is darkness, and their end is not being seen.”

“But Master Gotama, what is the aim of ascetics? What is their preoccupation? What is their support? What is their resolve? What is their end?”

“Brahmin, ascetics aim for patience and gentleness, are preoccupied with wisdom, their support is virtue, their resolve is possessionlessness, and their end is Nibbāna.”

“Wonderful, Master Gotama! Marvelous, Master Gotama! Master Gotama knows the aim, the preoccupation, the support, the resolve, and the end of khattiyas as well. Master Gotama knows those of brahmins... householders... women... thieves... and Master Gotama knows the aim, the preoccupation, the support, the resolve, and the end of ascetics as well.

Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”

The Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Appamāda Sutta

53. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One and exchanged friendly greetings with him.
320:
After exchanging pleasant and memorable greetings, he sat to one side. Sitting there, that brahmin said to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, is there one quality which, when developed and cultivated, secures both kinds of benefit—the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life?”

“Brahmin, there is one quality which, when developed and cultivated, secures both kinds of benefit—the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life.”

“But Master Gotama, what is that one quality which, when developed and cultivated, secures both kinds of benefit—the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life?”

“Brahmin, that one quality which, when developed and cultivated, secures both kinds of benefit—the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life—is heedfulness (appamāda).

“Brahmin, just as the footprints of all land-dwelling beings fit into the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant’s footprint is considered the chief among them because of its great size; even so, brahmin, heedfulness is the one quality which, when developed and cultivated, secures both kinds of benefit—the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life.

“Brahmin, just as all the rafters of a peaked house lead to the roof peak, slope towards the roof peak, and converge at the roof peak, and the roof peak is considered the chief among them; even so, brahmin... (as above) ...

“Brahmin, just as a cutter of pabbaja grass, having reaped the grass, takes it by the top and shakes it down, shakes it out, and beats it; even so, brahmin... (as above) ...

“Brahmin, just as when a cluster of mangoes is cut at the stalk, all the mangoes attached to the stalk follow it; even so, brahmin... (as above) ...

“Brahmin, just as all minor kings are followers of a Wheel-turning Monarch, and the Wheel-turning Monarch is considered the chief among them; even so, brahmin... (as above) ...

“Brahmin, just as the radiance of all the stars does not equal even a sixteenth part of the radiance of the moon,”
321:
"Just as the light of the moon is said to be the best among all those lights of the stars, Brahmin, even so, there is one quality which, when developed and cultivated, stands grasping both kinds of welfare—the welfare in this present life and the welfare in the life to come—that is, heedfulness (appamāda).

Brahmin, this is the one quality which, when developed and cultivated, stands grasping both kinds of welfare—the welfare in this present life and the welfare in the life to come."

"Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! ... May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts."

The eleventh discourse.

## 12. Dhammika Sutta

54. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha, on the Vulture Peak Mountain (Gijjhakūṭa).

At that time, the Venerable Dhammika was the resident monk in all seven monasteries in the district of Jātibhūmi. On that occasion, the Venerable Dhammika would abuse, revile, annoy, vex, and harass the visiting monks with speech. Those visiting monks, being abused, reviled, annoyed, vexed, and harassed with speech by the Venerable Dhammika, would depart for elsewhere, unable to stay, and would abandon the monastery.

Then the lay followers living in Jātibhūmi had this thought:

"We support the Saṅgha of monks with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Yet, the visiting monks depart for elsewhere, unable to stay, and abandon the monastery. What is the cause, what is the reason why the visiting monks depart for elsewhere, are unable to stay, and abandon the monastery?"

Then the lay followers living in Jātibhūmi had this thought again:

"This Venerable Dhammika abuses, reviles, annoys, vexes, and harasses the visiting monks with speech. Those visiting monks, being abused, reviled, annoyed, vexed, and harassed with speech by this Venerable Dhammika, depart for elsewhere, unable to stay, and abandon the monastery."
322:
"What if we were to expel the Venerable Dhammika?"

Then the lay followers living in Jātibhūmi approached the Venerable Dhammika and said to him: "Venerable sir, may the Venerable Dhammika depart from this monastery. Enough of your staying here."

Then the Venerable Dhammika went from that monastery to another monastery. There too, the Venerable Dhammika abused, reviles, annoyed, vexed, and harassed the visiting monks with speech. Those visiting monks, being abused, reviled, annoyed, vexed, and harassed with speech by the Venerable Dhammika, departed for elsewhere, unable to stay, and abandoned the monastery.

Then the lay followers living in Jātibhūmi had this thought again:

"We support the Saṅgha of monks with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. Yet, the visiting monks depart for elsewhere, unable to stay, and abandon the monastery. What is the cause, what is the reason why the visiting monks depart for elsewhere, are unable to stay, and abandon the monastery?"

Then the lay followers living in Jātibhūmi had this thought again:

"This Venerable Dhammika abuses, reviles, annoys, vexes, and harasses the visiting monks with speech. Those visiting monks, being abused, reviled, annoyed, vexed, and harassed with speech by the Venerable Dhammika, depart for elsewhere, unable to stay, and abandon the monastery. What if we were to expel the Venerable Dhammika?"

Then the lay followers living in Jātibhūmi approached the Venerable Dhammika and said to him: "Venerable sir, may the Venerable Dhammika depart from this monastery as well. Enough of your staying here."

Then the Venerable Dhammika departed from that monastery as well and went to another monastery. There too, the Venerable Dhammika abused, reviled, annoyed, vexed, and harassed the visiting monks with speech. Those visiting monks, being abused, reviled, annoyed, vexed, and harassed with speech by the Venerable Dhammika, departed for elsewhere, unable to stay, and abandoned the monastery.

Then the lay followers living in Jātibhūmi had this thought again:

"We support the Saṅgha of monks with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick..."
323:
“However, visiting monks depart, they do not stay, they abandon the monastery. What is the cause, what is the reason why visiting monks depart, do not stay, and abandon the monastery?” (This thought occurred to them).

Then, this thought occurred to the lay followers of his birthplace: “This Venerable Dhammika insults the visiting monks. ... [etc.] ... It would be good if we were to expel Venerable Dhammika from all seven monasteries in his birthplace for good.” (This thought occurred to them).

Then, the lay followers of his birthplace approached Venerable Dhammika and said to him: “Venerable sir, may Venerable Dhammika depart from all seven monasteries in his birthplace for good.”

Then, this thought occurred to Venerable Dhammika:
“The lay followers of my birthplace are expelling me from all seven monasteries in my birthplace. Where should I go now?” (This thought occurred to him).

Then, the thought occurred to Venerable Dhammika: “It would be good if I were to go to the Blessed One.”

Then, Venerable Dhammika took his bowl and robes and set out for Rājagaha. In due course, he arrived at Rājagaha, at Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, where the Blessed One was. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side. As Venerable Dhammika was sitting at one side, the Blessed One said to him:

“Come now, Brahmin Dhammika, from where have you come?”

“Venerable sir, the lay followers of my birthplace have expelled me from all seven monasteries in my birthplace,” (he replied).

“Enough, Brahmin Dhammika. What is the use of your staying in your birthplace? They expel you from this and that monastery. Being expelled from this and that monastery, you come only to me.”

“Brahmin Dhammika, in the past, sea-faring merchants would take a shore-sighting bird and set out to sea by ship. When the ship could not see the shore, they would release the shore-sighting bird. That bird would fly to the east, fly to the west, fly to the north, fly to the south, fly upwards, and fly to the intermediate quarters. If it saw the shore all around, it would fly there. If it did not see the shore all around, it would return only to that ship.”

“In the same way, Brahmin Dhammika, they expel you from this and that monastery. Being expelled from this and that monastery, you come only to me.”
324:
“If it does not see the shore all around, it returns only to that ship. In the same way, Brahmin Dhammika, they expel you from this and that monastery. Being expelled from this and that monastery, you come only to me.”

“Brahmin Dhammika, in the past, King Koravya had a Banyan tree-king named Suppatiṭṭha. It had five branches, provided cool shade, and was delightful. Brahmin Dhammika, the spread of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha was twelve yojanas, and the spread of its roots was five yojanas. Brahmin Dhammika, the fruits of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha were so large, like a rice pot holding one āḷhaka. Its fruits were as sweet as pure honey without larvae. Brahmin Dhammika, the king together with his harem enjoyed one branch of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha; the army enjoyed one branch; the townspeople and countryfolk enjoyed one branch; the ascetics and brahmins enjoyed one branch; and the animals enjoyed one branch. Brahmin Dhammika, no one guarded the fruits of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha, and they did not harm each other's fruits.”

“Then, Brahmin Dhammika, a certain man ate his fill of the fruits of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha, broke a branch, and departed. Then, Brahmin Dhammika, this thought occurred to the deity residing in the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha:

‘How wonderful, sirs! How marvelous, sirs! What an extremely evil man, in that he ate his fill of the fruits of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha, broke a branch, and departed. It would be good if the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha were not to give fruit in the future.’ (This thought occurred to the deity).

Brahmin Dhammika, then the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha did not give fruit in the future. Brahmin Dhammika, then King Koravya approached Sakka, the lord of the gods, and said this to him:

‘Please know, dear sir, that the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha no longer gives fruit.’

Brahmin Dhammika, then Sakka, the lord of the gods, performed such a feat of psychic power that a great wind and rain came and caused the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha to fall down with its roots turned upwards.”

“Brahmin Dhammika, the deity of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha, being miserable and dejected, stood at one side weeping with a tearful face.”

“Brahmin Dhammika, then Sakka, the lord of the gods, approached the deity of the Banyan tree-king Suppatiṭṭha and said this to him:

‘Deity, why are you standing at one side, miserable and dejected, weeping with a tearful face?’

‘Lord, a great wind and rain came and caused my abode to fall down.’”
325:
"[The wind] has uprooted it," she said, "and that is why I weep."

"Deity, did a great wind and rain come and topple your mansion, uprooting it, while you were standing in the 'tree-dhamma' (rukkha-dhamma)?"

"But sir, how does a tree stand in the 'tree-dhamma'?"

"Deity, in this world, those who need roots take the roots, those who need bark take the bark, those who need leaves take the leaves, those who need flowers take the flowers, and those who need fruit take the fruit. Because of such taking, the deity should not feel displeased or dissatisfied. In this way, deity, a tree stands in the 'tree-dhamma'."

"Sir, it was while I was not standing in the 'tree-dhamma' that a great wind and rain came and toppled my mansion, uprooting it."

"Deity, if you were to stand in the 'tree-dhamma', your mansion might be as it was before."

"Sir, I will stand in the 'tree-dhamma'; let my mansion be as it was before."

Then, Dhammika the Brahmin, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, performed such a feat of psychic power that a great wind and rain came and raised the Suppatiṭṭha banyan tree, and its roots became as they were before.

"In the same way, Dhammika the Brahmin, did the lay followers of your birthplace expel you from all seven dwellings in your birthplace while you were standing in the 'recluse-dhamma' (samaṇa-dhamma)?"

"But Bhante, how does a recluse stand in the 'recluse-dhamma'?"

"Dhammika the Brahmin, in this Dispensation, a recluse does not abuse in return when abused, does not annoy in return when annoyed, and does not quarrel in return when quarreled with. In this way, Dhammika the Brahmin, a recluse stands in the 'recluse-dhamma'."

"Bhante, it was while I was not standing in the 'recluse-dhamma' that the lay followers of my birthplace expelled me from all seven dwellings in my birthplace."

"Dhammika the Brahmin, in the past, there was a teacher named Sunetta, a founder of a sect, who was free from lust for sensual pleasures. Dhammika the Brahmin, the teacher Sunetta had many hundreds of disciples. The teacher Sunetta taught his disciples the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world. Dhammika the Brahmin, while the teacher Sunetta was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world, those disciples who did not have faith in their hearts, with the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell."
326:
"While the teacher Sunetta was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world, those disciples who had faith in their hearts, with the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.

Dhammika the Brahmin, in the past—

There was a teacher named Mūgapakkha... (and so on).

There was a teacher named Araṇemi... (and so on).

There was a teacher named Kuddālaka... (and so on).

There was a teacher named Hatthipāla... (and so on).

There was a teacher named Jotipāla, a founder of a sect, who was free from lust for sensual pleasures. Dhammika the Brahmin, the teacher Jotipāla had many hundreds of disciples. The teacher Jotipāla taught his disciples the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world.

Dhammika the Brahmin, while the teacher Jotipāla was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world, those disciples who did not have faith in their hearts, with the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell.

While the teacher Jotipāla was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahma world, those disciples who had faith in their hearts, with the breakup of the body, after death, were reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.

What do you think, Dhammika the Brahmin? If someone, with a corrupted mind, were to abuse or revile these six teachers, founders of sects, who were free from lust for sensual pleasures and had many hundreds of followers along with their assembly of disciples, would they not generate much demerit?"

"Yes, Bhante."

"Dhammika the Brahmin, if someone, with a corrupted mind, were to abuse or revile these six teachers, founders of sects, who were free from lust for sensual pleasures and had many hundreds of followers along with their assembly of disciples, they would generate much demerit.

However, someone who, with a corrupted mind, abuses or reviles a single person possessed of right view (a Sotāpanna) generates even more demerit than that.

Why is that?

Dhammika the Brahmin, I do not say that such abuse outside [this Dispensation] is as destructive to oneself as I say it is among fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī).

Therefore, Dhammika the Brahmin, you should train yourself thus:

'Our minds will not be corrupted towards our fellow practitioners.' This, Dhammika the Brahmin, is how you should train."

Sunetta, Mūgapakkha, and the Brahmin Araṇemi...
327:
Kuddālaka and the young Hatthipāla were also teachers. Jotipāla, named Govinda, who was the chaplain to seven kings, was also a teacher. These six famous teachers of the past were non-violent. Free from the 'raw scent' (of defilement), devoted to compassion, and having transcended the fetters of sensual desire, these teachers discarded sensual passion and passed on to the Brahma world.

The hundreds of disciples of those six teachers were also free from the 'raw scent' (of defilement), devoted to compassion, and had transcended the bonds of sensual fetters. Having discarded the 'sensual passion' (kāmarāga) for sensual pleasures, they passed on to the Brahma world.

If a person, with a mind of ill-will, abuses those recluses outside the Dispensation who are free from passion (through suppression) and are well-concentrated, such a person generates much demerit.

However, if a person, with a mind of ill-will, abuses a single monk, a disciple of the Buddha, who is endowed with (the path-knowledge of) right view, this person generates much more demerit than the one who abuses those six teachers.

One should not offend a person of good character (a Sotāpanna) who has abandoned the grounds for the sixty-two types of wrong views. This person, though not yet free from sensual passion, is called the seventh person of the Noble Saṅgha. For such a Sotāpanna, the five faculties are tender; faith, mindfulness, energy, tranquility, and insight are tender.
328:
By offending such a monk, one is said to harm oneself even before (harming another). Having harmed oneself, one then harms another. He who protects himself is said to protect the external enemy. Therefore, a wise person should always protect himself and not destroy (his own virtue).

The Twelfth Sutta.

## 6. Mahā Vagga

## 1. Soṇa Sutta

55. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha on Vulture's Peak Mountain. At that time, the Venerable Soṇa was staying at Rājagaha in the Cool Grove (Sītavana). Then, while the Venerable Soṇa was in seclusion and solitude, this thought arose in his mind:

"Among those disciples of the Blessed One who live with energetic effort, I am one. Yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. There is wealth in my family; I am able to enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds. What if I were to give up the training, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds?"

Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in Venerable Soṇa's mind with His own mind—just as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—disappeared from Vulture's Peak Mountain and appeared before Venerable Soṇa in the Cool Grove. The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Venerable Soṇa paid homage to the Blessed One and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him:

"Soṇa, while you were in seclusion and solitude, did not this thought arise in your mind: 'Among those disciples of the Blessed One who live with energetic effort, I am one. Yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. There is wealth in my family; I am able to enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds. What if I were to give up the training, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds?'"

"Yes, Bhante."

"Soṇa, what do you think? In the past, when you were a layman, were you not skilled in playing the lute?"

"Yes, Bhante."
330:
“Soṇa, what do you think? When you were formerly a layman, were you skilled in the sound of the lute's strings?”
“Yes, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were too taut, was your lute then tuneful or playable?”
“No, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were too slack, was your lute then tuneful or playable?”
“No, Bhante.”
“But when the strings of your lute were neither too taut nor too slack, but set at an even pitch, was your lute then tuneful or playable?”
“Yes, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Soṇa, over-energetic effort leads to restlessness, and over-lax effort leads to laziness. Therefore, Soṇa, resolve on the balance of effort, penetrate the equality of the faculties (such as faith, etc.), and therein take up the sign (of calm, etc.).”
“Yes, Bhante,” the Venerable Soṇa replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Soṇa with this instruction—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—disappeared from the Sītavana and appeared on Gijjhakūṭa Mountain.
Later, the Venerable Soṇa resolved on the balance of effort, penetrated the equality of the faculties, and therein took up the sign.
Then the Venerable Soṇa, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and having reached it, he dwelt therein. He knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.” And the Venerable Soṇa became one of the Arahants.
Then, to the Venerable Soṇa who had attained Arahantship, this thought occurred: “What if I were to approach the Blessed One and declare my attainment in his presence?” Then the Venerable Soṇa approached the Blessed One, paid homage, sat to one side, and addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Bhante, a monk who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal (the fruit of Arahantship), destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge, is dedicated to six things: he is dedicated to renunciation (the fruit of Arahantship);
331:
he is dedicated to seclusion (the fruit of Arahantship); he is dedicated to non-malice (the fruit of Arahantship); he is dedicated to the destruction of craving (the fruit of Arahantship); he is dedicated to the destruction of clinging (the fruit of Arahantship); he is dedicated to non-delusion (the fruit of Arahantship).

## 2. Phagguna Sutta

56. At that time, the venerable Phagguna was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, the venerable Phagguna is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit the venerable Phagguna out of compassion.”

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his solitary meditation and approached the venerable Phagguna. The venerable Phagguna saw the Blessed One coming from afar and made a gesture as if to rise from his bed.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Phagguna:

“Enough, Phagguna, do not move from your bed. There are these seats prepared by others; I will sit there.”

The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat and said to the venerable Phagguna:

“Phagguna, are you enduring? Are you getting by? Are your painful feelings subsiding and not increasing? Is their subsiding apparent and not their increase?”

“Venerable sir, I am not enduring, I am not getting by. My painful feelings are increasing and not subsiding. Their increase is apparent and not their subsiding.”
334:
"Venerable sir, just as if a strong man were to crush one's head with a sharp spike, even so, venerable sir, violent winds rack my head. Venerable sir, I am not enduring, I am not keeping going. My painful feelings are increasing, not decreasing; their increase is evident, not their decrease.

"Venerable sir, just as if a strong man were to tighten a tough leather thong around one's head, even so, venerable sir, I have severe headaches. Venerable sir, I am not enduring, I am not keeping going. My painful feelings are increasing, not decreasing; their increase is evident, not their decrease.

"Venerable sir, just as if a skilled butcher or a butcher's apprentice were to carve up the belly with a sharp butcher's knife, even so, venerable sir, violent winds carve up my belly.

"Venerable sir, just as if two strong men were to seize a weaker man by both arms and roast him, burn him over a pit of hot coals, even so, venerable sir, there is a fierce burning in my body. Venerable sir, I am not enduring, I am not keeping going. My painful feelings are increasing, not decreasing; their increase is evident, not their decrease."

Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the venerable Phagguna with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.

Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. ## 3. Chaḷabhijāti Sutta

57. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.
337:
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates six classes of birth: he designates the black class, the blue class, the red class, the yellow class, the white class, and the extremely white class.

In this regard, Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates as the black class: butchers of sheep, butchers of pigs, fowlers, hunters, deer-hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, jailers, and whoever else follow a cruel occupation.

Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates as the blue class: monks who live on thorns [lust and desire for the four requisites], and whoever else teach the efficacy of action and the efficacy of deeds.

Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates as the red class: the Nigaṇṭhas who wear a single cloth.

Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates as the yellow class: the white-robed lay disciples of the naked ascetics.

Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates as the white class: the Ājīvaka men and Ājīvaka women.

Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates as the extremely white class: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla. Venerable Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa designates these six classes of birth."

## 4. Āsava Sutta

58. "Monks, a monk endowed with six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. 

What are the six? 

Here, monks, a monk's taints that should be abandoned by restraint are abandoned by restraint; taints that should be abandoned by use are abandoned by use; taints that should be abandoned by endurance are abandoned by endurance; taints that should be abandoned by avoidance are abandoned by avoidance; taints that should be abandoned by removal are abandoned by removal; and taints that should be abandoned by development are abandoned by development. 

And what, monks, are the taints that should be abandoned by restraint, which are abandoned by restraint? 

Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, lives restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty. For, monks, while taints and the fever of distress might arise in one who lives without restraint of the eye faculty, those taints and the fever of distress do not arise in one who lives restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty. Reflecting wisely, [he lives restrained with the restraint of] the ear faculty... (p)... the nose faculty... the tongue faculty... the body faculty...
341:
...lives restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty. For, monks, while taints and the fever of distress might arise in one who lives without restraint of the mind faculty, those taints and the fever of distress do not arise in one who lives restrained with the restraint of the mind faculty. These, monks, are called the taints that should be abandoned by restraint, which are abandoned by restraint.

And what, monks, are the taints that should be abandoned by use, which are abandoned by use? 

Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, uses the robe only for protection against cold, for protection against heat, for protection against the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, and only for the purpose of covering the parts of the body that cause shame. 

Reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood not for fun, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for enrichment, but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: 'Thus I shall remove old feelings and not give rise to new feelings; and I shall have sustenance, blamelessness, and living in comfort.' 

Reflecting wisely, he uses the lodging only for protection against cold, for protection against heat, for protection against the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, and only for the purpose of removing the dangers of the seasons and for enjoying seclusion. 

Reflecting wisely, he uses medicinal requisites and equipment for the sick only for the protection against arisen painful feelings and for the sake of maximum freedom from suffering. 

Monks, while taints and the fever of distress might arise in one who does not use [these four requisites reflecting wisely], those taints and the fever of distress do not arise in one who uses them [reflecting wisely]. These, monks, are called the taints that should be abandoned by use, which are abandoned by use.

And what, monks, are the taints that should be abandoned by endurance, which are abandoned by endurance? 

Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, is one who endures cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; ill-spoken and unwelcome words; and he is one who endures arisen bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, piercing, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening. Monks, while taints and the fever of distress might arise in one who does not endure [such suffering], those taints and the fever of distress do not arise in one who endures them.
342:
Monks, these are called the taints that should be abandoned by enduring, which are abandoned by endurance.

And what, monks, are the taints that should be abandoned by avoiding, which are abandoned by avoidance? Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, avoids a wild elephant, a wild horse, a wild bull, a wild dog, a snake, a stump, a thorny place, a pit, a precipice, a cesspool, and a sewer. Wise companions in the holy life would suspect a monk of being in evil states if he sits in such improper seats, wanders in such improper resorts, and associates with such bad friends. That monk, reflecting wisely, avoids such improper seats, such improper resorts, and such bad friends. For, monks, while taints and the fever of distress might arise in one who does not avoid these things, they do not arise in one who avoids them. These, monks, are called the taints that should be abandoned by avoiding, which are abandoned by avoidance.

And what, monks, are the taints that should be abandoned by removing, which are abandoned by removal? Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, removes it, dispels it, and brings it to an end. Reflecting wisely, [he does not tolerate] an arisen thought of ill-will... [pe]... an arisen thought of cruelty... he does not tolerate, abandons, removes, dispels, and brings to an end whatever evil unwholesome states have arisen. For, monks, while taints and the fever of distress might arise in one who does not remove these things, they do not arise in one who removes them. These, monks, are called the taints that should be abandoned by removing, which are abandoned by removal.

And what, monks, are the taints that should be abandoned by developing, which are abandoned by development? Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment. Reflecting wisely, he develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of states... [pe]... the enlightenment factor of energy... the enlightenment factor of joy... the enlightenment factor of tranquility... the enlightenment factor of concentration... Reflecting wisely, he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment (pariccāga-vossagga) and matures into the leaning towards Nibbāna (pakkhandana-vossagga). For, monks, in one who does not rightly develop these seven factors of enlightenment, taints and the fever of distress might arise...
343:
...but in one who develops them, those taints and the fever of distress do not arise. These, monks, are called the taints that should be abandoned by developing, which are abandoned by development.

Monks, a monk possessed of these six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

The Fourth Sutta.

‘Venerable sir, from this day forward, I will give gifts to the Saṅgha.’ 

The Fifth Sutta. 

1. He makes a living through woodwork, thus he is called the householder Dārukammika. 

## 6. Hatthisāriputta Sutta 

60. Thus have I heard— 
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. 

At that time, many elder monks, after returning from their alms round after the meal, were sitting together in the circular pavilion and were discussing Abhidhamma. There, the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta kept interrupting the elder monks while they were discussing Abhidhamma. Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta:
345:
“Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta, do not interrupt the elder monks while they are discussing Abhidhamma. Let Venerable Citta wait until the end of the talk.” 

When this was said, the monks who were friends of Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta said to Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika: 
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, do not rebuke Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta. Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta is wise. Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta is capable of discussing Abhidhamma with the elder monks.” 

“Friends, it is difficult for those who do not know the minds of others to know this. Friends, here a certain person is very gentle, very humble, and very peaceful as long as he lives in dependence on the Teacher or a fellow monk in a position of a teacher. But when he is away from the Teacher and away from fellow monks in a position of a teacher, he lives in association with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and their followers. As he lives in association, being intimate, unrestrained, and devoted to talk, lust (rāga) corrupts his mind. With a mind corrupted by lust, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. 

Friends, suppose a grain-eating ox is tied with a rope or confined in a pen. Friends, if someone were to say, ‘This grain-eating ox will never again descend into the grain field,’ would he be speaking correctly?” 

“No, friend.” 

“Friends, it is possible that the grain-eating ox might break the rope or break out of the pen and then descend into the grain field once again. 

In the same way, friends, here a certain person is very gentle, very humble, and very peaceful as long as he lives in dependence on the Teacher or a fellow monk in a position of a teacher. But when he is away from the Teacher and away from fellow monks in a position of a teacher, he lives in association with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and their followers.”
346:
Lust overwhelms the mind of that person who lives associating [with others], having given up [seclusion], with faculties wide open, and frequently engaging in talk. With a mind overwhelmed by lust, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life. (1)

Friends, here in this world, some person, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. That monk lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the first jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life. Friends, just as if, at a great four-way crossroads, a heavy rain were to fall, the dust would disappear and mud would appear. Friends, would a person speaking thus be speaking rightly: "Now, dust will never again appear at this named four-way crossroads"?

Friend, a person speaking thus would not be speaking rightly. Friend, at this named four-way crossroads, people might pass by, or cattle might pass by, or the wind and sun might dry up the moisture; in such a case, there is a clear reason why dust would appear once again.

In the same way, friends, here in this world, some person, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna. That monk lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the first jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life. (2)

Friends, here in this world, some person, with the subsiding of thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra)... enters and dwells in the second jhāna. That monk lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the second jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life.

Friends, just as if there were a large reservoir not far from a village or town. If a heavy rain were to fall there, it would cause the shells, snails, gravel, and pebbles to disappear. Friends, would a person speaking thus be speaking rightly: "Now, shells, snails, gravel, or pebbles will never again appear in this named reservoir"?

Friend, such a statement would not be speaking rightly. Friend, in this reservoir, people might drink, or cattle might drink, or the wind and sun might dry up the moisture; in such a case, there is a clear reason why shells, snails, gravel, and pebbles would appear once again.
347:
In the same way, friends, here in this world, some monk, with the subsiding of thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra)... enters and dwells in the second jhāna. That person lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the second jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life. (3)

Friends, here in this world, some person, with the fading away of rapture (pīti)... enters and dwells in the third jhāna. That person lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the third jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life.

Friends, just as if a man who had eaten a delicious meal would not find a stale meal appealing. Friends, would a person speaking thus be speaking rightly: "Now, a meal will never again appeal to this named man"?

Friend, such a statement would not be speaking rightly. Friend, as long as that essence remains in the body of this man who ate the delicious meal, another meal will not be able to appeal to him. When that essence of what was eaten disappears, then there is a reason why that meal could once again appeal to him.

In the same way, friends, here in this world, some person, with the fading away of rapture (pīti)... enters and dwells in the third jhāna. That person lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the third jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life. (4)

Friends, here in this world, some person, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. That person lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the fourth jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life.

Friends, just as if there were a mountain lake, sheltered from the wind and without waves. Friends, would a person speaking thus be speaking rightly: "Now, waves will never again appear in this named lake"?

Friend, such a statement would not be speaking rightly. Friend, a fierce storm coming from the east might produce waves in that lake. A fierce storm coming from the west... a fierce storm coming from the north... a fierce storm coming from the south might produce waves in that lake; thus there is a reason.

In the same way, friends, here in this world, some person, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. That monk lives associating with monks, thinking, "I am a gainer of the fourth jhāna." ... He disavows the training and returns to the lower life. (5)

Friends, here in this world, some person, by not attending to any signs, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind (animitta-cetosamādhi).
348:
That person lives in association with monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians, thinking, 'I have attained the signless concentration of mind (animitta cetosamādhi).' While he lives in association, being unrestrained, open in his faculties, and devoted to talk, lust (rāga) corrupts his mind. With a mind corrupted by lust, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.

Friends, suppose a king or a royal minister, traveling on a long journey with a fourfold army, were to enter a certain forest grove for a single night's stay. There, the sound of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and the din of drums, lutes, conchs, and kettledrums would drown out the sound of crickets. Friends, if someone were to say, 'The sound of crickets will never appear again in this forest grove,' would that person be speaking rightly?"

"No, friend."

"Friend, it is possible that when the king or royal minister departs from that forest grove, the sound of crickets will appear once again. In the same way, friends, some person here, by not attending to any signs, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind (animitta cetosamādhi). He lives in association with monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians, thinking, 'I have attained the signless concentration of mind.' While he lives in association, being unrestrained, open in his faculties, and devoted to talk, lust (rāga) corrupts his mind. With a mind corrupted by lust, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.

Then, at another time, the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta renounced the training and returned to the lower life. Then the monks who were companions of Citta Hatthisāriputta went to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika and said to him: "How is it, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika? Did you know with your own mind the mind of Citta Hatthisāriputta, thinking, 'Citta Hatthisāriputta is an attainer of such and such meditative attainments, yet he will renounce the training and return to the lower life'? Or did the devas inform you of this matter, saying, 'Venerable sir, Citta Hatthisāriputta is an attainer of such and such meditative attainments, yet he will renounce the training and return to the lower life'?"

"Friends, I knew with my own mind the mind of Citta Hatthisāriputta, thinking, 'Citta Hatthisāriputta is an attainer of such and such meditative attainments, yet he will renounce the training and return to the lower life.' Also, the devas...
349:
...informed me of this matter, saying, 'Venerable sir, Citta Hatthisāriputta is an attainer of such and such meditative attainments, yet he will renounce the training and return to the lower life.'"

Then the monks who were companions of Citta Hatthisāriputta went to the Blessed One, prostrated themselves, and sat to one side. Sitting there, those monks said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, Citta Hatthisāriputta was an attainer of such and such meditative attainments, yet he has renounced the training and returned to the lower life."

"Monks, Citta will not long for the quality of renunciation (nekkhamma) for long."

Then, not long after, Citta Hatthisāriputta shaved off his hair and beard, put on saffron-dyed robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness. Then the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta, dwelling alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute, in no long time reached that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, having realized it for himself in this very life with direct knowledge. He understood: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being." And the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta became one of the Arahants.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Majjhe Sutta

61. Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. At that time, after the meal, when they had returned from their alms round, a discussion arose among many elder monks who were sitting together in the circular pavilion:

"Friends, this was said by the Blessed One in the Pārāyana, in 'The Questions of Metteyya':

'The sage who, having known both ends,
Does not cling to the middle,
Him I call a great man;
He has transcended the seamstress here.'

Friends, what is one end? What is the second end? What is the middle? What is the seamstress?"

When this was said, a certain monk said to the elder monks:

"Friends, the present individual existence (attabhāva) produced by contact is one end. The future individual existence rooted in contact is the second end...
350:
“The cessation of contact is the middle; craving is the seamstress. This is true; craving stitches those two (contact and the origin of contact) for the arising of this or that existence.

Friends, by this much, a bhikkhu understands through direct knowledge the things to be known through direct knowledge (the Four Noble Truths), and understands through full understanding the things to be fully understood (the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin). Having understood through direct knowledge what should be known through direct knowledge, and having fully understood what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, the past five aggregates are one end, the future five aggregates are the second end, the present five aggregates are the middle.

Craving is the seamstress. This is true; craving stitches those five aggregates for the arising of this or that existence. Friends, by this much, a bhikkhu understands through direct knowledge the things to be known through direct knowledge (the Four Noble Truths), and understands through full understanding the things to be fully understood. Having understood through direct knowledge what should be known through direct knowledge, and having fully understood what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, pleasant feeling is one end, painful feeling is the second end, equanimity (neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling) is the middle. Craving is the seamstress. This is true; craving stitches that feeling for the arising of this or that existence. Friends, by this much, a bhikkhu understands through direct knowledge the things to be known through direct knowledge (the Four Noble Truths), and understands through full understanding the things to be fully understood. Having understood through direct knowledge what should be known through direct knowledge, and having fully understood what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, name is one end, form is the second end, consciousness is the middle. Craving is the seamstress. This is true; craving stitches that name and form for the arising of this or that existence. Friends, by this much, a bhikkhu understands through direct knowledge the things to be known through direct knowledge (the Four Noble Truths), and understands through full understanding the things to be fully understood. Having understood through direct knowledge what should be known through direct knowledge, and having fully understood what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Venerable sirs, the six internal sense bases are one end, the six external sense bases are the second end, consciousness is the middle. Craving is the seamstress. This is true; craving stitches those sense bases for the arising of this or that existence. Friends, by this much, a bhikkhu understands through direct knowledge the things to be known through direct knowledge (the Four Noble Truths),”
351:
“...understands through full understanding the things to be fully understood. Having understood through direct knowledge what should be known through direct knowledge, and having fully understood what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, self-identity (sakkāya) is one end, the origin of self-identity is the second end, the cessation of self-identity (Nibbāna) is the middle. Craving is the seamstress. This is true; craving stitches that self-identity and its cause for the arising of this or that existence. Friends, by this much, a bhikkhu understands through direct knowledge the things to be known through direct knowledge (the Four Noble Truths), and understands through full understanding the things to be fully understood. Having understood through direct knowledge what should be known through direct knowledge, and having fully understood what should be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”

When this was said, another bhikkhu said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, we have all expressed our own inspirations according to our own wisdom. Friends, let us go to the Blessed One; having approached the Blessed One, let us report this matter to him. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so shall we remember it.”

“Very well, friend,” the elder bhikkhus replied to that bhikkhu.

Then the elder bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the elder bhikkhus reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation they had with all the bhikkhus, asking:
“Venerable Sir, whose word was well-spoken?”

“Bhikkhus, in a way, the words of all of you are well-spoken. However, listen to the meaning I intended in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Metteyya:

‘He who, having known both ends, 
Does not smear the middle with wisdom;
That person I call a great man,
For he has escaped the seamstress.’

Listen to that, pay close attention, and I will speak.”

“Yes, Venerable Sir,” the elder bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, the present individual existence (attabhāva) through the power of contact is one end. The future individual existence having contact as its root is the second end. The cessation of contact (Nibbāna) is the middle. Craving is the seamstress. This is true; craving stitches that contact and the origin of contact for the arising of this or that existence. Bhikkhus, by this much, a bhikkhu understands through direct knowledge the things to be known through direct knowledge (the Four Noble Truths),”
352:
"He knows the thing to be known by fully knowing it; having known the thing to be known by higher knowledge and fully knowing the thing to be known, he makes an end of suffering in this very life." (The Seventh Sutta).

## 8. Purisindriyañāṇa Sutta

62. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country together with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at a market town of the Kosalans named Daṇḍakappaka. Then the Blessed One left the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree on a prepared seat. Those monks entered the market town of Daṇḍakappaka to search for lodgings.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with many monks, approached the Aciravatī River to bathe. Having bathed in the Aciravatī River and come back out, he stood wearing a single robe, letting his body dry. Then a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:

"Friend Ānanda, how is it? Did the Blessed One declare Devadatta—'Devadatta is headed for a state of deprivation, headed for hell, bound to remain there for an aeon, incurable'—after having encompassed his entire mind, or was it declared in some other way?"

"Friend, the Blessed One declared it just so."

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, I approached the Aciravatī River together with many monks to bathe. Having bathed in the Aciravatī River and come back out, I stood wearing a single robe, letting my body dry.

At that time, venerable sir, a certain monk approached me and said to me:

'Friend Ānanda, how is it? Did the Blessed One declare Devadatta—Devadatta is headed for a state of deprivation, headed for hell, bound to remain there for an aeon, incurable—after having encompassed his entire mind, or was it declared in some other way?'

When this was said, venerable sir, I told that monk: 'Friend, the Blessed One declared it just so.'"

"Ānanda, that monk must be a new monk, not long ordained, or if he is an elder, he must be a fool, incompetent."
353:
"How could he fall into doubt regarding what I have declared definitively? Ānanda, I do not see any other single person whom I have declared after encompassing his entire mind in such a way as I have Devadatta.

Ānanda, as long as I saw in Devadatta even a hair-tip's worth of bright quality, I did not declare: 'Devadatta is headed for a state of deprivation, headed for hell, bound to remain there for an aeon, incurable.'

But, Ānanda, when I did not see in Devadatta even a hair-tip's worth of bright quality, then I declared: 'Devadatta is headed for a state of deprivation, headed for hell, bound to remain there for an aeon, incurable.'

Ānanda, suppose there were a cesspool more than a man's height deep, full of excrement to the brim. A man were submerged in it, including his head. Another man, desiring his welfare, desiring his benefit, desiring his safety, would want to pull him out of that cesspool. As he walked all around that cesspool, he would not see even a hair-tip's worth of that man not smeared with excrement by which he could take hold of him and pull him out. In the same way, Ānanda, when I did not see in Devadatta even a hair-tip's worth of bright quality, then I declared: 'Devadatta is headed for a state of deprivation, headed for hell, bound to remain there for an aeon, incurable.'

Ānanda, if you would like to listen, I will analyze the Tathāgata's 'Purisindriya' knowledges—the knowledge of the faculties of beings."

"It is the time for this, Blessed One; it is the time for this, Fortunate One, that the Blessed One should analyze the Purisindriya knowledges. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it."

"Then listen, Ānanda, and pay close attention; I will speak."

"Yes, venerable sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Here, Ānanda, I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own: 'This person has both wholesome qualities and unwholesome qualities.' At a later time, I understand that person by encompassing his mind with my own: 'This person's wholesome qualities have disappeared, and unwholesome qualities have become manifest. However, there is in this person a wholesome root that has not been cut off...'"
354:
"Wholesome states will manifest again from that wholesome root; in this way, this person will be of a nature not to decline in the future," thus he knows the mind of another with his own mind.

Ānanda, suppose there were seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind or sun, full of essence, and well-stored, and they are sown in a good field, in well-prepared soil. Ānanda, would you know: "These seeds will reach growth, increase, and abundance"?

"Yes, Bhante."

In the same way, Ānanda, I know a certain person here, encompassing his mind with my mind: "This person has both wholesome and unwholesome states."

At a later time, I know him, encompassing his mind with my mind: "The wholesome states of this person have disappeared, and unwholesome states have become manifest. However, he has an uncut wholesome root, and from that wholesome root, wholesome states will manifest again. In this way, this person will be of a nature not to decline in the future."

In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows an individual person by encompassing his mind with his mind.

In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the 'knowledge of the faculties of persons' (purisindriya-ñāṇa) by encompassing his mind with his mind.

In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the 'future arising of states' (āyatiṃ dhammasamuppāda) by encompassing his mind with his mind. (1)

Ānanda, I know a certain person here, encompassing his mind with my mind: "This person has both wholesome and unwholesome states." At a later time, I know him, encompassing his mind with my mind: "The unwholesome states of this person have disappeared, and wholesome states have become manifest. However, he has an uncut unwholesome root, and from that unwholesome root, unwholesome states will manifest again. In this way, this person will be of a nature to decline in the future."

Ānanda, suppose there were seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind or sun, full of essence, and well-stored, and they are placed on a large flat rock. Ānanda, would you know: "These seeds placed on the rock will not reach growth, increase, and abundance"?

"Yes, Bhante."

In the same way, Ānanda, I know a certain person here, encompassing his mind with my mind: "This person has both wholesome and unwholesome states."

At a later time, I know him: "The unwholesome states of this person have disappeared..."
355:
"...and wholesome states have become manifest. However, he has an uncut unwholesome root, and from that unwholesome root, unwholesome states will manifest again. In this way, this person will be of a nature to decline in the future," thus he knows the mind of another with his own mind.

In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows an individual person by encompassing his mind with his mind. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the 'knowledge of the faculties of persons' (purisindriya-ñāṇa) by encompassing his mind with his mind.

In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the 'future arising of states' (āyatiṃ dhammasamuppāda) by encompassing his mind with his mind. (2)

Ānanda, I know a certain person here, encompassing his mind with my mind: "This person has both wholesome and unwholesome states." At another time, I know him: "This person does not have even as much as the tip of a hair's breadth of bright state; this person is entirely possessed of dark, unwholesome states. With the breaking up of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell."

Ānanda, suppose there were seeds that are broken, rotten, and damaged by wind and sun, and they are sown in a good field, in well-prepared and ploughed soil. Ānanda, would you know: "These seeds will not reach growth, increase, and abundance"?

"Yes, Bhante."

In the same way, Ānanda, I know a certain person here, encompassing his mind with my mind: "This person has both wholesome and unwholesome states." At another time, I know him: "This person does not have even as much as the tip of a hair's breadth of bright state; this person is entirely possessed of dark, unwholesome states. With the breaking up of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell."

In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows an individual person by encompassing his mind with his mind.

In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the 'knowledge of the faculties of persons' (purisindriya-ñāṇa) by encompassing his mind with his mind. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the 'future arising of states' (āyatiṃ dhammasamuppāda) by encompassing his mind with his mind. (3)

When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

"Bhante, is it possible to designate another three persons who are similar to these three persons?"

"It is possible, Ānanda," the Blessed One said.

"Ānanda, I know a certain person here, encompassing his mind with my mind: 'This person has both wholesome and unwholesome states,'"
356:
At another time, encompassing that person's mind with my mind, I know: 'For this person, wholesome states have disappeared and unwholesome states have appeared. However, there is in him an unsevered root of the wholesome, but even that will be completely uprooted. In this way, this person will be of a declining nature in the future.'

Ānanda, suppose there were glowing coals, blazing and radiant, placed on a large flat rock. Would you know, Ānanda, that these coals will not reach growth, increase, and expansion?

Yes, Bhante.

Ānanda, or suppose in the evening when the sun is setting, would you know, Ānanda, that the light will disappear and darkness will appear?

Yes, Bhante.

Ānanda, or suppose at the time of the midnight meal, would you know, Ānanda, that the light has disappeared and darkness has appeared?

Yes, Bhante.

Ānanda, in the same way, here I know a certain person, encompassing his mind with my mind: 'For this person, there exist both wholesome and unwholesome states.' At another time, encompassing his mind with my mind, I know: 'For this person, wholesome states have disappeared and unwholesome states have appeared. However, there is in him an unsevered root of the wholesome, but even that will be completely uprooted. In this way, this person will be of a declining nature in the future.'

In this way too, Ānanda, a person is known by the Tathāgata by encompassing his mind with his mind. In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata's knowledge of the faculties of persons (purisindriya-ñāṇa) is known by encompassing mind with mind. In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata's knowledge of the future arising of states is known by encompassing mind with mind.

Ānanda, here I know a certain person, encompassing his mind with my mind: 'For this person, there exist both wholesome and unwholesome states.' At another time, encompassing his mind with my mind, I know: 'For this person, unwholesome states have disappeared and wholesome states have appeared. However, there is in him an unsevered root of the unwholesome, but even that will be completely uprooted. In this way, this person will be of a non-declining nature in the future.'

Ānanda, suppose there were glowing coals, blazing and radiant, placed on a heap of dry grass or a heap of wood. Would you know, Ānanda, that these coals will reach growth, increase, and expansion?
357:
"Yes, Bhante."

"Ānanda, just as at dawn when the sun is rising, would you know, Ānanda: 'Darkness will disappear and light will appear'?"

"Yes, Bhante."

"Ānanda, just as at midday, at the time of the morning meal, would you know, Ānanda: 'Darkness has disappeared and light has become manifest'?"

"Yes, Bhante."

"Even so, Ānanda, here I know a certain person by encompassing their mind with my own: 'For this person, there exist both wholesome states and unwholesome states.' At another time, I know that person by encompassing their mind with my own: 'For this person, unwholesome states have disappeared, and wholesome states have become manifest. However, there is in this person an unwholesome root that is not yet severed, but even that unwholesome root will be completely eradicated. In this way, this person will be of a nature not to decline in the future.'

Ānanda, in this way, the Tathāgata knows the individual person by encompassing their mind with his own.

Ānanda, in this way, the Tathāgata knows the 'knowledge of the faculties of persons' (purisindriyañāṇa) by encompassing their mind with his own.

Ānanda, in this way, the Tathāgata knows the 'arising of future states' by encompassing their mind with his own. (5)

Ānanda, here I know a certain person by encompassing their mind with my own: 'For this person, there exist both wholesome states and unwholesome states.' At another time, I know that person by encompassing their mind with my own: 'This person does not have even as much as a hair-tip's worth of unwholesome states; this person is endowed with states that are entirely bright and blameless; they will attain Parinibbāna in this very life.'

Ānanda, just as if cold, extinguished coals were placed on a heap of dry grass or a heap of wood. Would you know, Ānanda: 'These coals will not reach growth, increase, and expansion'?"

"Yes, Bhante."

"Even so, Ānanda, here I know a certain person by encompassing their mind with my own: 'For this person, there exist both wholesome states and unwholesome states.' At another time, I know that person by encompassing their mind with my own: 'This person does not have even as much as a hair-tip's worth of unwholesome states; this person is endowed with states that are entirely bright and blameless; they will attain Parinibbāna in this very life.'

Ānanda, in this way, the Tathāgata knows the individual person by encompassing their mind with his own. Ānanda, in this way, the Tathāgata knows the 'knowledge of the faculties of persons' (purisindriyañāṇa) by encompassing their mind with his own."
358:
Ānanda, in this way the Tathāgata, having discerned mind with mind, knows the future arising of the Dhamma [in a person]. (6)

Ānanda, among those first three persons, one is of a nature not to decline, one is of a nature to decline, and one is bound for the states of deprivation, for hell.

Ānanda, among those latter three persons, one is of a nature to decline, one is of a nature not to decline, and one is of a nature to attain final Nibbāna.

The Eighth Sutta.

In what connection was this said?

Monks, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear... smells cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, monks, are not sensual pleasures; in the discipline of the Noble One, they are called cords of sensual pleasure.

'The passion of intention is man's sensuality,
The beautiful things in the world are not sensuality;
The passion of intention is man's sensuality,
The beautiful things remain just as they are in the world,

And what, monks, is the origin of sensual pleasures? Contact (phassa), monks, is the origin of sensual pleasures.

And what, monks, is the diversity of sensual pleasures?
