Monks, what is the result of sensual desires?

Monks, one who desires sensual pleasures brings about a corresponding individual existence, whether partaking of merit or partaking of demerit. Monks, this is called the result of sensual desires.

Monks, what is the cessation of sensual desires?

Monks, the cessation of contact is the cessation of sensual desires.

This very Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of sensual desires.

What is it?

Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

'Monks, feeling should be known... the practice leading to the cessation of feeling should be known.' In reference to what was this said?

Monks, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Monks, what is the origin of feelings?

Monks, contact is the origin of feelings.

Monks, what is the diversity of feelings?

Monks, there is worldly pleasant feeling, there is unworldly pleasant feeling; there is worldly painful feeling, there is unworldly painful feeling; there is worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, there is unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Monks, this is called the diversity of feelings.

Monks, what is the result of feelings? One who experiences a feeling brings about a corresponding individual existence, whether partaking of merit or partaking of demerit...

Monks, this is called the result of feelings.

Monks, what is the cessation of feelings?

Monks, the cessation of contact is the cessation of feelings.

Right view... right concentration.

Monks, when a noble disciple understands feeling in this way, understands the origin of feelings in this way, understands the diversity of feelings in this way, understands the result of feelings in this way, understands the cessation of feelings in this way, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of feelings in this way, he then understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of feelings.

'Monks, feelings should be known... the practice leading to the cessation of feelings should be known.' What I have said was said in reference to this. (2)

'Monks, perception should be known... the practice leading to the cessation of perception should be known.' In reference to what was this said?

Monks, there are these six perceptions: perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of smells, perception of tastes, perception of tangibles, and perception of mental objects.

Monks, what is the origin of perceptions?

Monks, contact is the origin of perceptions.

Monks, what is the diversity of perceptions?

Monks, perception of forms is one thing, perception of sounds is another, perception of smells is another, perception of tastes is another, perception of tangibles is another, and perception of mental objects is another. Monks, this is called the diversity of perceptions.

Monks, what is the result of perceptions?

I say that perception results in expression. As one perceives a thing, so one expresses it: 'I had such a perception.' Monks, this is called the result of perceptions.

Monks, what is the cessation of perceptions?

Monks, the cessation of contact is the cessation of perceptions.
362:
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of perceptions. What is it? Right view... [p]... Right concentration. 

Monks, when a noble disciple thus understands perceptions, thus understands the origin of perceptions, thus understands the diversity of perceptions, thus understands the result of perceptions, thus understands the cessation of perceptions, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of perceptions, he then understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of perceptions. 

'Monks, perceptions should be known... [p]... the way leading to the cessation of perceptions should be known'—what was said thus was said in reference to this. (3)

'Monks, the taints (āsavas) should be known... [p]... the way leading to the cessation of the taints should be known'—in reference to what was this said? 

Monks, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). 

And what, monks, is the origin of the taints? Ignorance (avijjā), monks, is the origin of the taints. 

And what, monks, is the diversity of the taints? Monks, there are taints that lead to hell, there are taints that lead to the animal realm, there are taints that lead to the sphere of pretas, there are taints that lead to the human world, and there are taints that lead to the deva world. This, monks, is called the diversity of the taints. 

And what, monks, is the result of the taints? Monks, one who is immersed in ignorance brings about a corresponding individual existence (attabhāva) produced either by merit or by demerit. This, monks, is called the result of the taints. 

And what, monks, is the cessation of the taints? The cessation of ignorance, monks, is the cessation of the taints. 

This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. What is it? Right view... [p]... Right concentration. 

Monks, when a noble disciple thus understands the taints,
363:
thus understands the origin of the taints, thus understands the diversity of the taints, thus understands the result of the taints, thus understands the cessation of the taints, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of the taints, he then understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of the taints. 

'Monks, the taints should be known... [p]... the way leading to the cessation of the taints should be known'—what was said thus was said in reference to this. (4)

'Monks, kamma should be known... [p]... the way leading to the cessation of kamma should be known'—in reference to what was this said? 

Monks, it is intention (cetanā) that I call kamma. Having intended, one performs kamma by way of body, speech, or mind. 

And what, monks, is the origin of kamma? Contact (phassa), monks, is the origin of kamma. 

And what, monks, is the diversity of kamma? Monks, there is kamma to be experienced in hell, there is kamma to be experienced in the animal realm, there is kamma to be experienced in the sphere of pretas, there is kamma to be experienced in the human world, and there is kamma to be experienced in the deva world. This, monks, is called the diversity of kamma. 

And what, monks, is the result of kamma? Monks, I say that the result of kamma is threefold: that which is experienced in this very life, that which is experienced in the next life, or that which is experienced in some subsequent life. This, monks, is called the result of kamma. 

And what, monks, is the cessation of kamma? The cessation of contact, monks, is the cessation of kamma. 

This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of kamma. What is it? Right view... [p]... Right concentration. 

Monks, when a noble disciple thus understands kamma, thus understands the origin of kamma, thus understands the diversity of kamma, thus understands the result of kamma, thus understands the cessation of kamma, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of kamma, he then understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of kamma. 

'Monks, kamma should be known... [p]... the way leading to the cessation of kamma should be known'—what was said thus was said in reference to this. (5)

'Monks, suffering (dukkha) should be known, the origin of suffering should be known, the diversity of suffering should be known, the result of suffering should be known...'
364:
“The cessation of suffering should be known, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering should be known”—this was said. With reference to what was this said?

Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

Monks, what is the origin of suffering?
Monks, craving (taṇhā) is the origin of suffering.

Monks, what is the diversity of suffering?
Monks, there is suffering that is extreme, there is suffering that is slight, there is suffering that fades away slowly, and there is suffering that fades away quickly. Monks, this is called the diversity of suffering.

Monks, what is the result of suffering?
Monks, here in this world, someone overcome by suffering, with a mind obsessed, sorrows, pines, and laments; he beats his breast and becomes distraught, falling into bewilderment. Or else, overcome by suffering, with a mind obsessed, he searches outside: ‘Who knows a word or two (of a mantra) for the cessation of this suffering?’ Monks, I say that suffering has either bewilderment as its result or search as its result. Monks, this is called the result of suffering.

Monks, what is the cessation of suffering?
Monks, the cessation of craving is the cessation of suffering.

This very Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
What is it?
Right View... Right Concentration.

Monks, when a noble disciple understands suffering thus, understands the origin of suffering thus, understands the diversity of suffering thus, understands the result of suffering thus, understands the cessation of suffering thus, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of suffering thus, he understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of suffering.

“Monks, suffering should be known. The origin of suffering should be known, the diversity of suffering should be known, the result of suffering should be known, the cessation of suffering should be known, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering should be known”—this was said. It is with reference to this that it was said. (6)

Monks, this is the ‘Nibbedhika-pariyāya’ (Penetrative Exposition) Dhamma teaching. (The Ninth Sutta).

'All formations will appear to me as unstable.'
386:
'My mind will not delight in the whole world.'
'My mind will emerge from the whole world.'
'My mind will incline toward Nibbāna.'
'My fetters (saṃyojana) will be abandoned.'
'I will be endowed with supreme recluseship (the Noble Path).'

Monks, seeing these six benefits, it is enough for a monk to establish the perception of impermanence in all formations without limit.

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Ukkhittāsika Sutta

103. Monks, seeing six benefits, it is enough for a monk to establish the perception of suffering in all formations without limit.

What are the six?
'The perception of revulsion toward all formations will be established in me, just as toward a murderer with a raised sword.'
'My mind will emerge from the whole world.'
'I will see peace in Nibbāna.'
'My underlying tendencies (anusaya) will be uprooted.'
'I will be one who does what is to be done (the duty of a monk).'
'I will have served the Teacher with an act of love.'

Monks, seeing these six benefits, it is enough for a monk to establish the perception of suffering in all formations without limit.

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Atammaya Sutta

104. Monks, seeing six benefits, it is enough for a monk to establish the perception of non-self in all phenomena without limit.

What are the six?
'I will be uninvolved (atammaya) with the whole world (free from craving and views).'
'My notions of "I-making" (conceit/views) will cease.'
'My notions of "mine-making" (craving) will cease.'
'I will be endowed with uncommon knowledge (not shared by worldlings).'
'I will clearly see the causes.'
'I will clearly see the phenomena arisen from causes.'

Monks, seeing these six benefits, it is enough for a monk to establish the perception of non-self in all phenomena without limit.

The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Bhava Sutta

105. Monks, these three existences are to be abandoned, and one should train in the three trainings.

Which three existences are to be abandoned?
Sensual existence (kāma-bhava),
387:
fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava), and immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava)—these three existences are to be abandoned.

In which three trainings should one train?
In the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), in the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and in the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā)—in these three trainings one should train.

Monks, when a monk has abandoned these three existences and has completed the training in these three trainings, he is called a monk who has cut off craving, discarded the fetters, and by the right breakthrough of conceit, has made an end of suffering.

The Tenth Sutta.

## 11. Taṇhā Sutta

106. Monks, these three cravings are to be abandoned, and these three conceits are to be abandoned.

Which three cravings are to be abandoned?
Craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā)—these three cravings are to be abandoned.

Which three conceits are to be abandoned?
Conceit (māna—based on birth, etc.), inferiority conceit (omāna), and over-conceit (atimāna)—these three conceits are to be abandoned.

Monks, when a monk has abandoned these three cravings and these three conceits, he is called a monk who has cut off craving, discarded the fetters, and by the right breakthrough of conceit, has made an end of suffering.

The Eleventh Sutta.

The Tenth Chapter on Benefits is finished.
388:
The second fifty suttas are finished.

## 6-Assāda Sutta

112. Monks, there are these three things. What are the three? The view of gratification (assāda-diṭṭhi), the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) which follows the personality, and wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) consisting of the sixty-two views. Monks, these are the three things. Monks, to abandon these three things, three things should be developed. What are the three? To abandon the view of gratification (assāda-diṭṭhi), the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) should be developed. To abandon the view of self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā) should be developed. To abandon wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) should be developed. ## 7-Arati Sutta

113. Monks, there are these three things. What are the three? Discontent (arati), harassment (vihiṃsā), and unrighteous conduct (akusala-kammapatha). Monks, these are the three things.

Monks, for the abandoning of these three things, these three things should be developed.
